Upon co-treatment with low-dose H 2 O 2 (1 mM), Zn-CN exerts excellent antibacterial activity against both Gram-negative Escherichia coli and Gram-positive Staphylococcus aureus by catalyzing ROS production to induce bacterial oxidative damage. The antibacterial efficacy was confirmed by colony counting, live/dead fluorescence staining, and intracellular ROS detection assays. This work provides a facile, energy-efficient approach for constructing neutral-pH active carbon nanozymes, offering a promising non-antibiotic platform to combat bacterial infections and antibiotic resistance.

works.title: Interface-specific functional coatings for soft-tissue integration of craniofacial implants: oral mucosa, percutaneous skin, and muscle
works.abstract: Soft tissue integration (STI) is essential for limiting inflammation, maintaining craniofacial implant stability, and supporting long-term function. This narrative review evaluates functional coatings at three distinct interfaces: oral mucosa around dental abutments, craniofacial muscle and enthesis around temporomandibular joint (TMJ) prostheses, and skin around percutaneous implants. We distinguish direct integrative effects from infection control and immunomodulation, and appraise evidence from cellular responses through tissue-level outcomes. Oral mucosa requires a rapid epithelial and connective-tissue seal under continuous plaque exposure; percutaneous skin requires suppression of epithelial downgrowth and pocket formation across a chronically exposed breach; and muscle-facing temporomandibular joint components require enthesis-like anchorage and load transfer under repetitive motion. The evidence is strongest for cell-level responses and selected preclinical mucosal or skin outcomes, whereas coating-mediated TMJ muscle attachment remains at proof-of-concept stage in non-TMJ models. Negative animal findings further show that favorable cell behavior or added antibacterial activity does not necessarily produce a durable tissue seal. Interface-specific coatings should therefore be designed around a primary tissue-level endpoint, with antimicrobial and immunomodulatory functions treated as supportive and dose-limited.

works.title: 3D droplet-based microphysiological niches drive early maturation transcriptional remodeling in human iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes
works.abstract: Human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CMs) are widely used for cardiac disease modeling and drug screening but remain limited by immature phenotypes and the inability of conventional culture systems to precisely control extracellular matrix (ECM) cues at single-cell resolution. Here, we present a Matrigel-containing microfluidic droplet platform for single-cell hiPSC-CM culture. Droplets were produced by flow-focusing, enabling single-cell encapsulation, controlled matrix exposure, live-cell imaging, and downstream molecular analysis. Systematic optimization identified 10% and 30% Matrigel dilutions as the optimal ECM concentration for bulk hiPSC-CMs culture in 2D plate format promoting hiPSC-CMs spreading and elongation. Encapsulation of 30% Matrigel in droplets maintained >80% hiPSC-CMs viability during 24-h on-chip culture. Using bulk RNA sequencing of cells pooled from droplets we show that 24-h 3D droplet culture induced a distinct transcriptional state compared with conventional 2D culture and freshly encapsulated 3D droplet control. Differential gene and pathway enrichment analyses revealed activation of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and ATP biosynthesis programs, alongside activation of early tissue-like cardiovascular signaling and remodeling pathways. These findings indicate that controlled ECM presentation in uniform 3D droplet microenvironment can initiate early metabolic maturation-associated transcriptome remodeling in hiPSC-CMs. Collectively, this work establishes a droplet-based platform for hiPSC-CM culture providing a foundation for next-generation microphysiological systems used in cardiac disease modeling, cardiotoxicity screening, and mechanistic studies of cardiomyocyte maturation.

works.title: Correction: A novel approach to promote upper-limb motor recovery in stroke survivors using assistive myoelectric control and adaptive visual feedback in virtual reality
Case Report: prolonged sinus tract formation after collagen-hydroxyapatite artificial bone grafting — diagnostic dilemma between infection and foreign body reaction
works.abstract: Prolonged sinus tract after artificial bone grafting presents a diagnostic and therapeutic dilemma. We report a case with 8-month longitudinal follow-up, propose a theoretical residual graft load (RGL)—inflammatory threshold (IT) balance framework to explain the recurrent “healing-rupture” pattern, and demonstrate a dual-phase dexamethasone strategy—as diagnostic tool and healing catalyst—after infection is excluded. A 38-year-old male developed fracture-related infection after left tibial plateau fracture fixation and was treated with the Masquelet technique. After second-stage grafting with artificial bone which was composed of bovine Type I collagen and hydroxyapatite mixed with autologous bone, the wound developed an aseptic sinus tract that persisted for 8 months. Repeated cultures were negative and inflammatory markers remained normal. At hardware removal, the graft showed “bean-curd-like” disintegration, suggesting foreign body reaction. Dexamethasone led to sinus healing, with recurrence after withdrawal confirming the diagnosis. As drainage gradually decreased, a final short course of dexamethasone resulted in complete wound closure. This case highlights that foreign body reaction, not infection, should be considered in such prolonged sinus tracts, and that the RGL—IT hypothesis provides a framework for understanding the healing-rupture cycle.

works.title: Design and theoretical assessment of Ti-Mo-Nb-Sn alloys for biomedical applications: a review
works.abstract: Biomaterials include a wide range of materials, including metals, ceramics, polymers, and composites. Of these, metallic materials are the most widely used, with titanium and its alloys being chosen for the medical field, particularly in orthopedics and dentistry, owing to their favorable weight-to-strength ratio, high mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and biocompatibility. However, titanium in its pure form does not always provide an optimal compromise between strength, elastic modulus, and microstructural stability, so alloying with biocompatible elements is used to fine-tune its mechanical and biological properties. First- and second-generation titanium implant alloys nonetheless present recognized limitations, including an elastic modulus considerably higher than that of cortical bone, which produces stress shielding, and the potential toxicity of the Al and V alloying elements used in Ti-6Al-4V. These shortcomings have driven sustained interest in metastable β-type titanium alloys stabilized by non-toxic elements such as Mo, Nb, Ta, Zr, and Sn. This review reorganizes current knowledge of the Ti-Mo-Nb-Sn system around the requirements such an alloy must satisfy, the individual and combined roles of Mo, Nb, and Sn as β-stabilizers, the compositions reported in the literature, the structure-to-property relationships that govern their mechanical behavior, and the methods used to assess their corrosion resistance and biocompatibility, concluding with the principal research gaps and future perspectives for this alloy family. The reviewed studies reported elastic moduli of about 49–65 GPa for single-β compositions, with yield strengths comfortably surpassing 200 MPa, with values of 400–975 MPa. Data regarding the biological profile exists for only one composition, and more information is inferred from related ternary alloys. Windows of 4–6 Mo, 11–20 Nb, and 6–9 Sn wt.% looking promising, but fatigue, wear resistance and long-term biological data are missing.

works.title: Reprogramming neural repair through the convergence of gene editing and bioelectronic scaffolds
works.abstract: Neural repair research increasingly combines molecular interventions with engineered environments that support axonal growth and circuit function. This narrative review examines neuronal growth pathways, direct cellular reprogramming, conductive scaffolds, extracellular-vesicle delivery, and neuroimmune and neurovascular interactions. Genetic studies of PTEN/mTOR, SOCS3/STAT3, and growth-associated transcription factors provide a biological foundation for investigating targeted gene regulation. CRISPR-based editing and transcriptional control offer distinct tools for exploring these pathways. Conductive and stimulus-responsive materials provide experimental interfaces for structural guidance, electrical stimulation, and local molecular delivery. Their integration with gene-regulatory systems is presented as a conceptual strategy for coordinating molecular and biophysical interventions. Organoids, single-cell and spatial profiling, and electrophysiological measurements offer complementary approaches to characterizing cell identity and network responses. Clinical studies targeting axon-growth inhibition provide a separate translational evidence stream, with outcomes interpreted according to intervention, injury characteristics, and trial design. Priorities for integrated repair systems include cell-specific delivery, material stability, durable circuit function, and longitudinal safety assessment. A prospective digital-twin workflow is proposed to connect biological measurements with computational predictions and experimentally evaluated intervention choices. Together, these research directions support a framework for studying programmable neural repair across molecular, cellular, and systems levels.

works.title: Fatigue-aware alveolar stress and strain tracking: a theoretical biomechanics framework for regional mechanical dose accumulation in ventilator-induced lung injury
works.abstract: Ventilator-induced lung injury remains incompletely explained by global bedside variables that do not resolve regional load, deformation, time, repetition, and recovery. FAAST (Fatigue-Aware Alveolar Stress and Strain Tracking) and its deterministic implementation, FAAST2, describe regional mechanical exposure and fatigue. The framework maps a shared central-airway boundary into 20 compartments, defines functional-residual-capacity-referenced volumetric strain, closes generalized constitutive stress through regional specific elastance, and tracks Time-Accumulated Stress History (TASH), the complete-cycle load-time channel, and Strain-Accumulated Strain History (SASH), the cumulative positive loading-branch deformation-work channel. A cycle-indexed Continuum of Damage Index (CDI) combines elemental load-time and deformation-work increments with inherited fatigue. CDI is irreversible and bounded; a continuous recovery-opportunity factor accelerates decay of reversible fatigue memory rather than subtracting accumulated damage. Applying selected ventilation values from Park’s ALS report with declared PEEP and normal-lung mechanics produced a chronic-stability comparator with 1-h Strain-Accumulated Strain History 88.9 kPa, dynamic strain 0.194, per-cycle deformation work 0.098 kPa, recovery opportunity 0.827, and bounded steady fatigue 0.015; CDI was not extrapolated across chronic support. Relative to this comparator, 1-h regional SASH across Cases 1–4H was 99.5, 485.1, 723.8, and 1,510.4 kPa, or 1.12, 5.46, 8.14, and 17.0 times the comparator, respectively; illustrative 24-h maximum compartment CDI was 0.280, 0.478, 0.618, and 0.851. Higher tidal volume increased burden despite fewer breaths, while a preferentially loaded compliant region in heterogeneous ARDS carried the greatest burden. A matched OSCILLATE sensitivity applied reported day-1 arm settings to the same Panwar-H-anchored 20-compartment lung for 24 h. In the compartment attaining maximum CDI at 24 h, control ventilation produced Time-Accumulated Stress History 28.080 kPa·h, SASH 15,496 kPa, and maximum compartment CDI 0.596. Across declared HFOV tracheal oscillatory tidal-volume sensitivities of 0.5–2.0 mL/kg predicted body weight, TASH was approximately 31.299 kPa·h, SASH ranged from 13,513 to 54,053 kPa, and CDI ranged from 0.575 to 0.777. Modeled SASH arm equivalence occurred at 0.573 mL/kg; this is a mechanical comparison point, not an injury threshold. These are ecological sensitivity outputs, not measured HFOV tidal volumes, patient reconstructions, time-weighted exposures, mortality predictions, or evidence that pulmonary mechanics exclude hemodynamic harm. FAAST2 requires regional construct validation and biological calibration before clinical use.

works.title: Multi-planar intersegmental coordination differs between retrained and habitual non-rearfoot strikers
works.abstract: Purpose This study aimed to compare multi-planar shank-foot coordination patterns and variability during stance between runners who transitioned from a rearfoot strike (RFS) to a non-rearfoot strike (NRFS) through gait retraining (RETs) and habitual NRFS runners (HABs). Methods Thirty-eight runners (18 RETs, 20 HABs) were analyzed. Multi-planar shank-foot coordination patterns and coordination variability (CV) were quantified across three key couplings using a modified vector coding technique. Sagittal-plane and impact-related outcomes, coordination-pattern proportions, and CV were analyzed using independent-samples tests, Mann-Whitney U tests, and generalized linear mixed models, respectively. Results Primary analyses showed no statistically significant between-group differences in foot-strike angle, peak vGRF, VALR, or VILR. Covariate-adjusted sensitivity analyses identified lower VALR and VILR in RETs ( P = 0.040 and P = 0.025). Coordination-pattern proportions differed during P4 of the shank transverse vs. foot sagittal coupling, with RETs exhibiting greater anti-phase distal-dominant and lower in-phase distal-dominant coordination. Significant group × phase interactions in CV were observed across all three couplings ( P ≤ 0.002), with greater CV in RETs during P2 of the shank frontal vs. foot sagittal coupling ( P = 0.021). Conclusion Phase- and coupling-specific differences in shank-foot coordination were observed between HABs and RETs who completed gait retraining and demonstrated an NRFS pattern at testing. Multi-planar coordination analysis may therefore provide complementary information beyond foot-strike classification and selected sagittal-plane or external loading measures.

works.title: Post-release handling and administration preserve the quality of adipose-derived mesenchymal stromal cell products across multiple delivery systems
works.abstract: Introduction Mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) are used clinically across regenerative and inflammatory indications, yet post-release steps including thawing, reconstitution, short room-temperature (RT) holds, and administration remain variably standardized and poorly documented. Post-release handling often occurs outside GMP oversight despite its potential impact on cell quality. Methods This study evaluated the impact of clinically relevant post-release handling conditions on adipose-derived MSCs (AD-MSCs) using in vitro models simulating common administration routes. AD-MSCs from three healthy donors were tested under four conditions: (1) baseline after reconstitution, (2) immediate administration, (3) 4-h RT storage, and (4) 4-h RT storage followed by administration. Five administration routes were simulated and evaluated independently using clinically relevant delivery systems. Viability, morphology, aggregation, debris, and immunophenotype were assessed using NucleoCounter analysis, microscopy, and flow cytometry. Results Cell counts remained stable across all conditions and administration routes. Viability exceeded the predefined acceptance criterion (≥80%) throughout, with the only significant change observed after 4-h storage in the intravenous administration system (mean viability 93.8% ± 1.0% at baseline versus 90.6% ± 2.7% after 4 h storage). Debris and aggregation remained below 10% across all conditions, indicating minimal fragmentation and clumping risk. Immunophenotype was preserved following storage (CD73/CD90/CD105 ≥90%; negative markers ≤1%). Morphology remained spindle-shaped, although reduced plastic adherence was observed after 4-h storage and passage through the intradiscal administration system. Needle-based administration across a clinically relevant range (21G-27G) had no adverse impact on viability, morphology, or aggregation. Discussion Post-release handling and administration maintained AD-MSC quality within predefined acceptance criteria across all evaluated delivery systems. Although small route-dependent changes were observed, none exceeded established quality thresholds. These findings support the robustness of the evaluated post-release handling procedures and provide a pragmatic quality-control framework for assessing maintenance of AD-MSC quality attributes during administration.

Characteristic metabolite emergence and coordinated multi-omics reprogramming in a four-member synthetic Streptomyces consortium during rice straw deconstruction
Sequential regulation of dual catalytic modules for the directed biosynthesis of 2,5-furandicarboxylic acid in Escherichia coli
works.abstract: Bioconversion of 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF) to 2,5-furandicarboxylic acid (FDCA) confers advantages of mild conditions, high selectivity, and eco-friendliness. However, enzymatic catalysis is expensive and multi-strain microbial catalysis is limited by the transmembrane transport of intermediates between strains, restricting the efficient synthesis of FDCA and generating a byproduct. In this study, we aimed to establish sequential regulation of dual catalytic modules in Escherichia coli to precisely control the expression of hydroxymethylfurfural oxidase (HMFO) and vanillin dehydrogenase (VDH1), enabling the directed one-pot conversion of HMF to FDCA with no detectable accumulation of the measured intermediates and simplifying the operational process. At a 15 mM HMF scale, this strategy achieved a FDCA yield of 100%, significantly higher than the 78.6% yield of the dual-enzyme cascade system established by HMFO and VDH1, and the 56.73% yield from the dual-strain catalysis constructed by two engineered E. coli strains that harbor either hmfo or vdh1(Student's t-test, p < 0.0001). Furthermore, at a laboratory scale (production of a fermentation broth containing 100 g of FDCA), life cycle assessment demonstrated sequential regulation of dual catalytic modules represented the lowest environmental impact among the three systems (dual-strain catalysis and dual-enzyme cascade). It reduced global warming potential, fossil fuel depletion, and ecotoxicity by 70-82% compared with the other two systems. Overall, this study establishes a more efficient and sustainable strategy for directed FDCA biosynthesis.

works.title: Integrated simultaneous fermentation–pervaporation for intensified bioethanol production and recovery in a corn stover cascade biorefinery
works.abstract: Corn stover was valorized through an integrated cascade biorefinery combining subcritical water pretreatment, enzymatic hydrolysis, alcoholic fermentation, and pervaporation for intensified bioethanol production and recovery. Subcritical water treatment effectively solubilized the hemicelluloses while increasing cellulose accessibility in the solid residue. This enabled glucose yields of approximately 80% after 24 h of enzymatic hydrolysis. The resulting hydrolysate was then used in two strategies for the production and recovery of bioethanol. In the first one, the glucose-rich liquid was efficiently fermented by Saccharomyces cerevisiae, achieving complete glucose consumption within 15 h and an ethanol yield of 91%. Subsequently, ethanol was recovered through pervaporation, where silicone membranes were identified as the most suitable option due to their superior permeation performance. A novel integrated simultaneous fermentation-pervaporation (SFP) approach was developed as the second strategy to intensify bioethanol production and recovery by coupling both processes in a single operation. Operating the hybrid process at 38 °C substantially enhanced ethanol removal, allowing 98% of the produced ethanol to be recovered within only 15.3 h, compared with 60% recovery achieved by the sequential strategy. SFP at 38 °C achieved the highest overall yield, reaching 97% and demonstrated that integrating fermentation and pervaporation at this temperature effectively improved ethanol recovery and process productivity, providing a promising approach for sustainable lignocellulosic biorefineries.

works.title: Adaptive laboratory evolution of Cupriavidus necator to sodium salts as a whole cell engineering strategy for enhanced trehalose production
works.abstract: Trehalose is an important compatible solute with diverse applications in the pharmaceutical, food, and cosmetic industries. In Cupriavidus necator, trehalose biosynthesis is naturally associated with osmotic stress, but typically retained intracellularly as an osmo-protectant. In this study, adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) was used as a whole cell engineering strategy to adapt C. necator H16 to increasing osmotic stress. ALE was performed with independent lineages and gradually increasing concentrations of NaCl and Na₂SO₄, reaching stable growth at up to 500 mM NaCl or 400 mM Na₂SO₄. In selected single colonies of the adapted cultures, the SetA sugar efflux transporter from Escherichia coli was expressed to enable trehalose secretion. Moderate concentrations of Na₂SO₄ were identified as most effective osmotic trigger, balancing growth and trehalose production. Under the selected production conditions the best-performing adapted isolate produced 11.5 g/L trehalose from 20 g/L fructose, corresponding to 60.5% of the theoretical maximum yield, compared to 7.4 g/L and 42.1% in the parental strain. Genome sequencing revealed mutations affecting transporters, membrane structure, metabolism and regulators. These mutations are considered contributors to the observed osmoadaptive phenotype, while individual effects on trehalose production were not resolved. Overall, the results demonstrate the potential of ALE as a whole cell engineering strategy for generating C. necator isolates with improved extracellular trehalose production under defined conditions. Cupriavidus necator H16 was adapted to increasing NaCl and Na2SO4 concentrations by ALE with final concentrations of 500 mM NaCl and 400 mM Na2SO4. ALE was used as a whole cell engineering strategy with subsequent selection for osmotic-stress resistance. In the adapted isolate, the trehalose exporter SetA was expressed using a plasmid. Moderate Na2SO4 concentrations of 150 mM provided an effective osmotic trigger for enhanced trehalose production. The selected NaCl-adapted isolate produced 11.5 g/L trehalose from 20 g/L fructose. Genome sequencing revealed mutations in genes potentially associated with osmoadaptation.

works.title: Bacillus subtilis as a heterologous host for production and secretion of a hyperthermostable archaeal subtilisin-like protease
works.abstract: Abstract Pernisine is a subtilisin-like protease from the hyperthermophilic archaeon Aeropyrum pernix . Its ability to degrade resistant protein substrates such as prion proteins makes this protease attractive for industrial applications. Here, we used Bacillus subtilis as a heterologous host for expression and secretion prepropernisine, a precursor of pernisine. The native secretion signal peptide of prepropernisine was replaced with a signal peptide of native B. subtilis preprosubtilisin E to achieve efficient secretion. Among the four promoters tested, xylose-inducible promoter yielded the highest level of propernisine production, with a titer of 175 mg per l of culture. The produced propernisine was purified from the culture medium using a combination of ultrafiltration, anion-exchange chromatography, and heat treatment. Approximately 115 mg of propernisine with 80% purity was obtained per liter of culture, representing a 10-fold higher yield than previously achieved with other heterologous hosts. Activated pernisine obtained from B. subtilis exhibited remarkably high thermostability, with optimal activity at temperatures above 90 °C and across a pH range of 7 to 9. In addition, it retained approximately 60% of initial activity after autoclaving and efficiently degraded collagen and meat. The stability and performance of pernisine from B. subtilis were nearly identical to that of pernisine produced in Escherichia coli . Overall, these findings demonstrate that B. subtilis is a promising host for further optimization of cultivation conditions and scale-up to controlled bioreactor cultivation, to achieve production of pernisine at industrial level. Key points • Bacillus subtilis efficiently produced and secreted recombinant propernisine. • Propernisine was readily purified from the culture medium. • Activated pernisine exhibited high thermostability and efficient meat hydrolysis.

works.title: Theoretical georeferenced potential for biomethane production in Brazil from organic waste, including logistics and cost aspects
works.abstract: Abstract One of the challenges for biomethane production in Brazil, as well as its use, is related to transportation logistics, owing to the lack of detailed studies of the entire supply chain at a national level, which includes all the stages from waste collection to transportation for its final use. In addition, the lack of adequate logistics and infrastructure for biomethane can make its production economically unfeasible. Given this, this article aims to present a study of the potential for producing biomethane from animal manure, sewage sludge, and vinasse from sugar cane and corn, considering its end use, biogas production costs, and purification technologies, using the Geographic Information Systems method for georeferencing. ArcGIS Pro 3.7 software was used to study logistics and create biomethane potential and cost maps. Amine scrubbing was the most efficient technology, at around 97.02%. With this technology, a biomethane production potential of 1.101 billion m 3 per year was estimated from the total waste studied in Brazil. However, water scrubbing had the lowest specific production cost for plants with capacities greater than 500 m 3 h −1 , around 29.97 US$ MWh −1 for a 2000 m 3 h −1 plant, considering transportation by truck and 33.97 US$ MWh −1 considering the same size plant and direct injection into the natural gas network. Considering the average price of natural gas in Brazil in 2024 of 68.87 US$ MWh −1 , biomethane proved to be economically viable from a capacity of 500 m 3 h −1 using water scrubbing, pressure swing adsorption, and membrane separation technologies, and from 700 m 3 h −1 with amine scrubbing technology. This shows that it is economically possible to produce biomethane in some regions of Brazil when the logistics are adequately exploited.

works.title: Mainstream anammox strengthened by capacitive ammonium enrichment: Enhanced nitrogen conversion and reorganization of the PN/A microbial community
Transesterification of triolein and methanol via a solid-in-oil suspension to produce methyl oleate
In Focus: Materials and the Environment Symposium ( XXXIII IMRC , México)
Extremozymes producing halophilic microbiota as an effective tool in bioremediation of synthetic dyes from the environment
works.abstract: Abstract Synthetic dyes represent a category of organic compounds that are highly stable, durable, and often resistant to degradation through natural processes. These dyes are produced and utilized globally across various industrial sectors, where they are applied to color different substrates by adhering to their surfaces. A significant concern arises from their release into watercourses and soils during manufacturing, processing, and dyeing activities. Compared to physical–chemical methods, the bioremediation of environments contaminated with synthetic dyes through biological approaches is generally more feasible, cost‐effective, and ultimately more efficient. Microorganisms employ three primary mechanisms to eliminate dyes from wastewater and soil: biosorption, bioaccumulation, and enzymatic biodegradation. Among microorganisms, halophilic bacteria and archaea are particularly attractive for bioremediation because of their ability to thrive under hypersaline conditions, metabolic versatility, and production of robust enzymes involved in dye degradation. Recent studies have identified haloarchaea as especially promising candidates for the treatment of saline industrial effluents due to their exceptional tolerance to salt stress, and other harsh environmental conditions. Because industrial wastewaters typically exhibit elevated salinity, non‐halophilic microorganisms may be less effective or entirely ineffective in remediation efforts. A promising alternative therefore lies in the application of halophilic microorganisms, which are naturally found in marine environments, salt lakes, or anthropogenic environments resulting from salt mining and processing. This review explores various aspects of synthetic dye remediation using halophilic microorganisms, detailing the mechanisms involved and providing insights into the production and potential application of recombinant extremozymes for addressing these environmental challenges. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry (SCI).

works.title: Revealing fermentation pathway of methane-to-organic acid bioconversion by aerobic methanotrophs
works.abstract: Bioconversion of methane to value-added liquid chemicals is a sustainable strategy to alleviate reliance on crude oil. Here, this study uncovers an efficient pathway for converting methane into organic acids, including acetic and formic acids, through aerobic methanotrophs. Under nitrogen-limiting conditions, methane is assimilated into intracellular storage compounds (glycogen or polyhydroxybutyrate), which are subsequently fermented into organic acids under oxygen-limiting conditions. This two-stage process is conserved across both Type I ( Methylococcus capsulatus Bath, 8326 μmol organic acids/g dry cell weight (DCW)) and Type II ( Methylosinus sp . LW4, 946 μmol organic acids/g DCW) methanotrophs in batch culture. Using 13 C-labelling and proteomics, carbon flux and functional genes were confirmed in this pathway, while transmission electron microscopy visualized the accumulation and consumption of intracellular storage compounds. By using the proven efficient fermentation pathway, this study further applied M. capsulatus Bath in both semi-continuous and continuous bio-fermenters and demonstrated sustained methane-to-organic acid conversion over 90 days. These findings unveil a likely universal fermentation strategy among aerobic methanotrophs, which can serve as a new platform for sustainable biological production of organic acids from methane feedstocks

works.title: A data-driven framework for modeling, interpretation, and multi-objective surrogate optimization of dairy spray drying using heterogeneous literature data
works.abstract: Simultaneous control of dairy powder quality during spray drying is challenging because feed composition, processing conditions, and powder properties interact nonlinearly. This study developed a unified machine learning framework integrating prediction, interpretation, and multi-objective optimization using heterogeneous literature-derived datasets comprising 110–178 observations per target from 35 studies. Four regression models were evaluated for yield, final moisture content, median particle size, and residual thermal ratio using nested leave-one-out cross-validation, with imputation and hyperparameter tuning performed within each fold. XGBoost achieved the highest R² for yield (0.679), moisture (0.781), and thermal ratio (0.921), whereas random forest performed best for particle size (0.799); differences from competing models were within uncertainty except for thermal ratio. Leave-one-study-out validation revealed limited cross-study transferability: R² decreased to 0.523 for moisture, 0.307 for particle size, and 0.223 for thermal ratio, while yield predictions did not generalize across studies. Out-of-sample model interpretation identified physically plausible process–quality relationships and discrepancies from training-set attributions. Multi-objective optimization generated 200 Pareto-optimal candidate conditions; incorporating applicability-domain and particle-size constraints increased predicted specification compliance from 6.5% to 100%. However, broad jackknife+ prediction intervals, whose coverage falls below nominal for unseen studies, and the absence of independent experimental validation preclude conclusions about operational reliability. The principal contribution is a methodological framework for synthesizing dispersed literature data to explore process trade-offs and guide experimental design. The framework identifies candidate operating regions that require independent experimental validation before operational deployment.

works.title: UV photolysis of extracellular antibiotic resistance genes: degradation, deactivation, and implications for resistance control
Nanophotonic biosensors for environmental monitoring of chemical and microbiological residues
works.abstract: Environmental monitoring has made significant strides in recent years; however, despite remarkable progress, reliable on-site detection and continuous monitoring of contaminants remain challenging. Besides well-known chemical pollutants, the increasing presence of emerging contaminants in complex environmental samples has raised global concerns regarding their negative effects on human health and ecosystems. This situation underscores the need for efficient continuous monitoring and portable analytical tools that can conduct in-field and on-site analyses to detect and quantify relevant pollutants in complex environmental samples. Nanophotonic sensors are becoming powerful analytical platforms for environmental monitoring due to their high sensitivity, rapid response, label-free detection capabilities, potential for multiplexing, and compatibility with on-chip integration and miniaturization. This review provides an overview of recent advances in nanophotonic sensor technologies, including plasmonic and silicon photonic sensors, for the environmental monitoring of industrial chemicals, pharmaceutical residues, toxic by-products, microplastics, and microbiological agents. It examines key developments in device integration and multi-analyte detection strategies, highlighting representative applications across different classes of contaminants in water sources, along with selected gas-sensing examples. It also discusses current challenges and future prospects for decentralized environmental monitoring.

works.title: Engineering integrated portable and microfluidic platforms for on-site PFAS monitoring
works.abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are widely used for their anti-adhesive, waterproofing, and surfactant properties, but their persistence, ubiquity, and toxicity raise major concerns for environmental and human health. Conventional PFAS analysis relies on chromatographic and mass spectrometry-based methods that, although highly sensitive, require centralized laboratories, expensive instrumentation, and time-consuming procedures. This has motivated the development of portable sensing platforms and microfluidic systems for on-site monitoring. This review examines recent engineering advances in portable and microfluidic technologies for PFAS detection in water, including optical and electrochemical sensing approaches and their integration into miniaturized analytical platforms. Particular attention is given to analytical performance, sensing principles, and suitability for environmental samples. Current systems show promise for rapid field screening and hotspot identification, but limitations in selectivity, sensitivity, matrix compatibility, and regulatory validation still restrict their practical deployment. Consequently, these technologies are best positioned as complementary tools to established laboratory-based analytical methods.

works.title: L-Threonine production from acetate by metabolically engineered Corynebacterium glutamicum using a pH-controlled fed-batch process
works.abstract: Acetate has a considerable potential as a non-food feedstock for microbial bioproduction, yet its use for amino acid production remains underexplored. Here, we developed a process for L-threonine production from acetate as the sole carbon source with Corynebacterium glutamicum by integrating rational, genome-based metabolic engineering with pH-coupled fed-batch cultivation. The engineered strain AT-3 carried five chromosomal mutations that alleviated feedback inhibition of key enzymes and redirected carbon flux toward the aspartate pathway. Substrate supply was controlled using a custom Visual Basic-based feeding script that automatically adjusted the acetic acid feed in response to online pH measurements. Robust process performance was maintained during a tenfold scale-up from 100-mL DASbox to 1-L DASGIP bioreactors. The optimized process achieved an L-threonine titer of 10.04 g/L and a yield of 0.086 g/g acetate. This study provides a basis for further studies on the development and improvement of acetate-based amino acid production process. KEY POINTS: • Plasmid-free C. glutamicum strains produce L-threonine in acetate minimal medium • pH-controlled acetic acid feed in bioreactors improved L-threonine production • Acetate-based production of feed amino acids avoids competition with human food.

works.title: Nitrogen-doped carbon dots for combating bacterial infections via synergistic membrane disruption and biofilm eradication
works.abstract: Nitrogen-doped carbon dots (N-CDs) have emerged as promising antibacterial nanomaterials. In this work, a series of N-CDs with varying nitrogen doping levels (0%–20%) were synthesized via a one-step hydrothermal method using D-sorbitol and L-lysine as precursors, targeting the growing challenge of bacterial infections. The resulting samples were characterized by transmission electron microscopy (TEM), atomic force microscopy (AFM), Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy, ultraviolet–visible (UV-Vis) absorption and fluorescence spectroscopy, Raman spectroscopy, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), and Zeta potential/particle size analysis. The effects of nitrogen doping on the structural, optical, physicochemical, and antibacterial properties were systematically investigated. The 15% N-CDs exhibited optimal antibacterial activity against Escherichia coli ( E. coli) and Staphylococcus aureus ( S. aureus ), with inhibition rates of 95.32% ± 1.41% and 91.61% ± 1.36%, respectively, while showing excellent biocompatibility toward normal mammalian cells (HUVEC and HT-22) up to 700 μM. Mechanistic studies revealed that the optimal 15% N-CDs adhere to bacterial surfaces, disrupt cell membrane integrity, and inhibit biofilm formation (up to 81.1% ± 0.13% and 76.94% ± 0.24%), as evidenced by SEM, live/dead staining, and leakage assays. Collectively, these findings establish N-CDs as a promising nanoplatform that tackles bacterial infections through a synergistic membrane-damaging and biofilm-suppressing mechanism, without compromising mammalian cell viability.

works.title: Smart biomaterials for immunomodulation in periodontitis: advances and challenges
works.abstract: Periodontitis is a chronic immunoinflammatory disease characterized by irreversible periodontal tissue destruction. Its progression is closely associated with immune dysregulation and abnormal activation of immune cell subsets. Increasing attention has been directed toward immunotherapy to improve the limited regenerative capacity of periodontal tissues. Smart biomaterials can sense local periodontal signals and produce spatiotemporal responses for controlled drug release and modulation of the immune microenvironment. However, current research mainly focuses on material design and optimization, whereas systematic comparisons and clinical evaluations of responsive systems remain insufficient. This review summarizes recent advances in smart biomaterials for periodontal immunomodulation, with emphasis on their classification based on endogenous and exogenous stimuli. Challenges involving material stability, biosafety, controlled release, and clinical translation are also discussed. This review may provide insights into the future development of immunomodulatory therapies for periodontitis.

works.title: A vision-guided robotic platform for mechanical loading, ultrasound-visible tissue deformation assessment, local and systemic tolerability evaluation in rat and mouse skeletal muscle
works.abstract: Controlled and reproducible mechanical stimulation is essential for preclinical mechanotherapy research, yet existing small-animal loading systems often lack integrated anatomical targeting, force control, tissue-level mechanical assessment, and tolerability evaluation. We developed a vision-guided desktop robotic platform integrating RGB-D-based anatomical localization, real-time force sensing, closed-loop force control, and ultrasound-based tissue deformation assessment. The platform was evaluated in 24 male Sprague-Dawley rats and 24 male C57BL/6 mice across two anatomical regions and graded loading conditions. Body-surface-area scaling was used only as a geometric reference for loading-head dimensions, whereas loading-force ranges were selected from previous robotic mechanotherapy studies and preliminary observations. Rats received 0.6, 0.8, or 1.0 N loading to the tibialis anterior region, and mice received 0.1, 0.2, or 0.4 N loading to the bilateral cervical muscle region. Ultrasound imaging demonstrated force-related increases in tissue deformation area in both species, confirming that prescribed external force produced measurable tissue-level mechanical responses. Repeated loading for 14 days elicited behavioural responses, particularly in mechanical withdrawal thresholds and rotarod performance, although responses varied across endpoints and loading conditions. Local assessment showed no overt tissue injury, while muscle-fibre cross-sectional area, collagen-positive area, and CD31-positive signals changed with loading. Body weight, haematological indices, serum biochemical markers, and major-organ histology showed no consistent loading-related adverse changes, whereas serum cytokines exhibited limited, species-dependent variation. Overall, the platform enables reproducible force-controlled mechanical loading together with quantitative assessment of ultrasound-visible tissue deformation and provides a standardized experimental framework for investigating mechanical loading-tissue response relationships in small-animal mechanotherapy research.

works.title: Fungi-engineered metal nanoparticles for advanced therapeutics
works.abstract: Growing concern over the environmental toxicity and biomedical risks of conventional physical and chemical nanoparticle synthesis has intensified interest in sustainable routes to metal nanoparticle production. Myconanotechnology, which uses fungi as biological nanofactories, has emerged as a versatile green platform: fungi tolerate high metal concentrations and secrete abundant enzymes, proteins, and polysaccharides that act as reducing, stabilizing, and capping agents. Most existing reviews catalog producer species and nanoparticle types; here we instead integrate synthesis mechanisms, the physicochemical determinants of particle properties, and biomedical performance, and we weigh the strength of evidence behind each application. Antimicrobial and anticancer activities are currently the best supported, although the evidence is dominated by in vitro models, whereas vaccine-adjuvant and biosensing applications remain preliminary and mechanistically underdefined. Across silver, gold, copper, zinc, iron, and selenium systems, fungal biomolecules govern not only metal-ion reduction but also surface chemistry, biocompatibility, and immunological behavior, which distinguishes mycogenic NPs from plant-derived and chemically synthesized counterparts. The main barrier to translation is not a shortage of candidate materials but the absence of standardized, mechanistically informed synthesis and characterization protocols, which prevents batch-to-batch reproducibility and meaningful cross-study comparison. Closing this reproducibility gap, through defined culture conditions, quantitative surface characterization, and harmonized safety testing, is the most critical prerequisite for advancing fungi-engineered nanoparticles toward clinical and industrial use.

works.title: Material-dependent viscoelastic performance of TPU and PEBA gyroid intervertebral disc replacements under quasi-static and cyclic compression
works.abstract: Thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) and polyether block amide (PEBA) offer different mechanical profiles for additively manufactured intervertebral disc replacements. This study compared single-material Gyroid structures with the same nominal anatomically derived L4/L5 geometry using a harmonized secondary analysis of original specimen-level datasets. Geometry #08 comprised a 6 mm unit-cell size and a nominal wall thickness of 0.75 mm without a peripheral wall. FlexHard and FlexMed TPU and Spectrum and SainSmart PEBA were investigated. Three additional unloaded reference specimens per material underwent dimensional, gravimetric, and microscopic characterization. FlexHard, FlexMed, and Spectrum met the predefined quasi-static screening criterion of 4000–8000 N at 50% compression, whereas SainSmart remained below 4000 N and was not dynamically tested. Eligible groups completed 700,000 compression cycles between 600 and 2000 N at 5 Hz without apparent mechanical failure (n = 3 per material). Outcomes were evaluated over the final 600,000 cycles following 100,000 conditioning cycles. Structural stiffness increased by 16.1% for FlexHard and 76.5% for FlexMed but decreased by 10.6% for Spectrum. Apparent storage modulus increased by 30.9% and 44.1% in the TPU groups and decreased by 10.3% in Spectrum. Mean loss modulus increased in both TPU groups and decreased in Spectrum, although within-material changes were not significant after multiplicity adjustment. Tan δ and specific damping capacity decreased in all three groups, with both TPU formulations maintaining higher mean damping capacities than Spectrum. Immediately after loading, TPU specimens retained approximately 90% of their initial height, compared with approximately 95% for Spectrum; all groups recovered to approximately 97%–99% after 24 h. These exploratory findings identify complementary profiles in load support, energy dissipation, cyclic adaptation, and recovery. Because manufacturing conditions differed between source datasets, the results characterize the investigated material–manufacturing combinations and support joint optimization of formulation, processing, and architecture.

works.title: OTS ‐grafted zeolite membranes for diclofenac removal by air‐gap membrane distillation: from electrostatic to thermal retention mechanism
works.abstract: Abstract BACKGROUND The hydrophobic functionalization of ceramic membranes represents a promising strategy for pharmaceutical wastewater treatment. However, the relationship between surface chemistry and operating mode remains insufficiently understood. In this study, a zeolite microfiltration membrane with a mean pore size of 0.55 μm was grafted with n‐octadecyltrichlorosilane ( OTS ) to investigate the influence of surface hydrophobicity on filtration and air‐gap membrane distillation ( AGMD ) performance. RESULTS OTS grafting transformed the membrane surface from superhydrophilic (contact angle: 0°) to highly hydrophobic (120° ± 1.8°), as supported by thermogravimetric analysis, SEM – EDX , porosity measurements, N 2 adsorption–desorption analysis, and dry‐storage stability evaluation. During pressure‐driven filtration at 1 bar and ambient temperature, the grafted membrane exhibited low diclofenac ( DCF ) rejection (8.9%), while conductivity removal decreased from 62.6% for the ungrafted membrane to 41.1% after grafting. In contrast, AGMD operated at a feed temperature of 60 °C and a coolant temperature of 5 °C achieved 92.04% DCF rejection from the synthetic solution. For real pharmaceutical wastewater, apparent UV ‐based removal reached 86.42%, while chemical oxygen demand ( COD ) and conductivity removals were 96.45% and 88.97%, respectively. These findings are consistent with the expected separation mechanism of AGMD , although partial pore wetting or liquid leakage cannot be excluded. Water rinsing recovered 62.09% of the initial permeability, whereas sequential alkaline–acid cleaning restored it to 97.12% while largely preserving the hydrophobic surface (contact angle: 113.2° ± 2.3°). CONCLUSION Combining OTS ‐induced surface hydrophobicity with the thermal driving force of AGMD substantially improved contaminant retention compared with pressure‐driven filtration. The results highlight the potential of natural zeolite‐based ceramic membranes for pharmaceutical wastewater treatment and demonstrate the importance of appropriate cleaning strategies for permeability recovery. Further investigation of membrane wetting and liquid leakage is required to confirm long‐term separation performance and operational reliability. © 2026 The Author(s). Journal of Chemical Technology and Biotechnology published by John Wiley & Sons Ltd on behalf of Society of Chemical Industry (SCI).

works.title: Long-term carbon-limited operation of a pilot-scale high-MLSS anoxic–oxic reciprocating MBR: integrated removal of organic matter, nutrients, and micropollutants
A Rational Computational Pipeline for the Discovery of a Potent EGF-Mimetic Ligand with In vitro Enhanced Proliferative Activity in Cancer Stem Cells
Mechanistic understanding and optimization of moisture transport of Geniotrigona thoracica honey through clay pot wall
Biomass to bioenergy transition through sustainable bioconversion and circular bioeconomy strategies
works.abstract: Access to modern electricity and clean cooking technologies remains uneven across much of Africa, despite the continent's abundant biomass resources, which have the potential to enhance energy security while supporting the transition toward a circular bioeconomy. However, a substantial proportion of agricultural, forestry, municipal, and marine organic residues is still treated as waste rather than valorized within the formal energy sector. Morocco exemplifies this disconnect. Although the country has achieved near-universal rural electrification, biomass derived from agricultural and marine resources contributes less than 2% of the modern energy mix, highlighting that the principal challenge lies not in resource availability but in the development of efficient conversion pathways and integrated deployment strategies. This review examines recent advances in biomass-to-bioenergy technologies, with particular emphasis on sustainable bioconversion processes, including enzymatic hydrolysis, microbial fermentation, anaerobic digestion, and microbial fuel cells. Beyond evaluating technological progress, we assess research trends, innovation dynamics, and technology transfer through bibliometric and patent analyses to identify leading research areas, emerging technologies, and geographical disparities across Africa. We further discuss the role of life cycle assessment in evaluating the environmental sustainability of biomass conversion pathways and demonstrate its importance in identifying low-carbon alternatives capable of reducing greenhouse gas emissions. We conclude that Africa's energy sovereignty depends on moving away from generic policies toward integrated, country-specific deployment strategies that prioritize locally available biomass within circular bioeconomy frameworks.

works.title: Engineering all human milk oligosaccharide fucosidic linkages in planta
works.abstract: Human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs) are a component of breast milk which improve infant health outcomes by modulating immune responses, inhibiting pathogen adhesion, and promoting healthy gut microbiota. Although their effects are well-documented, few HMOs have been clinically or biochemically studied because only a handful of the simplest HMOs out of >200 species are currently possible to chemically synthesize or produce in microbes via metabolic engineering in microbial hosts. In contrast, plants are naturally adept at biosynthesizing a wide range of complex polysaccharides, and they have recently been established as a heterologous system for HMO production. However, much of the structural diversity of HMOs has not yet been reproduced in a plant, particularly fucosylations. Four fucosidic linkages can be found in fucosylated HMOs, but only Fucα1-2Gal has been biosynthesized in planta. Here, we screened bacterial fucosyltransferases using the model plant Nicotiana benthamiana to produce 3-fucosyllactose (Fucα1-3Glc), lacto-N-fucopentaose II (Fucα1-4GlcNAc), and lacto-N-fucopentaose III (Fucα1-3GlcNAc), demonstrating that all four fucosidic linkages can be made in planta. Just twelve glycosidic linkages make up all the HMOs found in breast milk, and our findings increase the number of linkages made in planta from seven to ten, greatly expanding the variety of HMOs accessible in a plant.

works.title: Characterization of the lysine-forming saccharopine dehydrogenase Lys1 from filamentous fungi
works.abstract: Abstract Lysine biosynthesis in fungi proceeds through the α-aminoadipate pathway with Lys1 (EC 1.5.1.7) catalyzing the final reversible L-lysine producing step. Although Lys1 from Saccharomyces cerevisiae has been characterized, limited information is available on this highly conserved enzyme in filamentous fungi relevant for solid-state food fermentation. Here, we compare Lys1 homologs from Aspergillus nidulans, Penicillium roqueforti, and Rhizopus microsporus with the S. cerevisiae enzyme as reference using phylogenetic, biophysical, kinetic, and molecular dynamics analyses. Sequence and structural comparisons showed sequence divergence across fungal lineages while overall fold and key catalytic residues were conserved. All enzymes displayed strong directional pH dependence, with the forward L-lysine producing reaction favored at alkaline pH and the reverse reaction promoted at neutral pH. Analyses of temperature profile revealed homolog-specific differences, with the homolog from S. cerevisiae presenting the highest temperature optimum and melting temperature. The turnover (kcat) of the reverse reaction was consistently higher than the forward reaction for all homologs, consistent with thermodynamic constraints on lysine formation. Kinetic characterization revealed that the S. cerevisiae enzyme had the highest kcat, followed by A. nidulans and P. roqueforti, whereas the R. microsporus enzyme had lower activity and highest activation energy. Molecular dynamics simulations corroborated that the more active homologs more frequently sampled near-reactive NAD⁺ C4-saccharopine C8 geometries, while R. microsporus showed lower sampling frequency of these conformations and weaker protein–ligand contact organization. These findings provide a mechanistic and kinetic basis for understanding lysine biosynthesis in filamentous fungi. Key points • Phylogenetic, biophysical, kinetic, molecular dynamics of Lys1 from fungi • Catalytic residues and Lys1 folds are conserved (LDDT > 0.9) but sequences differ • Reaction direction (saccharopine ↔ L-lysine) is strongly dependent on pH

works.title: Understanding the molecular-level responses of cattle rumen microbiota to kaolin clay as a feed additive in vitro
works.abstract: Abstract Enteric methane emissions from ruminants, primarily produced by methanogenic archaea during rumen fermentation, contribute substantially to greenhouse gas emissions and represent a loss of dietary energy. Clay mineral-based feed additives have been explored as potential methane mitigation strategies; however, their mechanisms remain poorly understood. This study investigated the mechanistic role of halloysite–kaolinite mixed mineral (kaolin) supplementation in modulating rumen fermentation and microbial functional potential, including bacteria, protozoa, and archaea, using an in vitro system. Approximately 5% clay was incorporated into 2 g of basal diet and incubated under anaerobic conditions using ANKOM technology. Samples were collected at defined intervals up to 48 h, and integrated 16S and 18S rRNA sequencing, and PICRUSt2 functional prediction analyses. Clay supplementation reduced methane by ~21%, from 35.43 ± 3.50 to 27.85 ± 2.31 mL CH 4 /g dry matter. Although bacterial and archaeal community composition shifted in response to supplementation, the dominant bacterial taxa ( Firmicutes and Bacteroidota ), and protozoal populations were largely preserved. Predicted methanogenesis pathway abundance was significantly reduced by ~47% ( p < 0.01), alongside methane reduction. Predicted functional analysis further revealed potential alteration in enzyme-mediated hydrogen utilisation ( p < 0.001). This might indicate a redistribution of metabolic hydrogen among competing pathways without accumulation. Microscopic observations further showed spatial associations between microbial cells and clay surfaces. These findings suggest that kaolin reduces methane production through changes in predicted functional potential related to methanogenesis and hydrogen utilisation, alongside shifts in bacterial and archaeal community composition, while fermentation-related parameters remained largely stable. Key points • Kaolin clay in feed suppresses rumen methanogenesis without disrupting fermentation or fibre digestion. • Clay may redirect hydrogen away from methane production, offering a practical methane-mitigation strategy. • Direct microbial attachment to clay coincided with altered predicted methanogenesis potential, while dominant taxa were largely preserved.

works.title: Rhizopus stolonifer as a biocatalyst for cyclic dipeptide production and artemisinin/artemether biotransformation
works.abstract: Abstract Fungi are prolific producers of chemically diverse natural products and biocatalytically active enzymes, yet the biosynthetic and biotransformation potential of many fungal species remains underexplored. This study establishes Rhizopus stolonifer as a promising platform for both natural-product discovery and selective biotransformation of bioactive molecules. Ten cyclic dipeptides (CDPs) and over seventy additional metabolites were tentatively identified using an integrated metabolomics approach combining gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry, and one- and two-dimensional nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. Three major CDPs, cyclo(L-Leu-L-Pro), cyclo(L-Ile-L-Pro), and cyclo(L-Phe-L-Pro), were subsequently isolated and characterized, with their stereochemical configurations established. In parallel, R. stolonifer was utilized as a microbial platform for the biotransformation of antimalarial drugs artemisinin and artemether. The resulting derivatives were generated through deoxygenation, site-selective hydroxylation, and structural rearrangement. Time-course NMR analyses provided evidence for the proposed biotransformation pathways. Genome mining revealed six putative non-ribosomal peptide synthetase biosynthetic gene clusters and thirteen cytochrome P450 monooxygenases, suggesting a genetic basis for CDP biosynthesis and artemisinin biotransformation, respectively. These results underscore the dual utility of R. stolonifer as a rich source of CDPs and a versatile biocatalyst for the transformation of artemisinin derivatives. Key points Rhizopus stolonifer is a rich source of cyclic dipeptides (CDPs). R. stolonifer biotransforms artemisinin and artemether into multiple derivatives. Non-ribosomal peptide synthetase pathways may underpin CDP production.

works.title: Prospective role of proteolytic microorganisms from fermented foods in degradation of gluten and their implications for celiac disease
works.abstract: Abstract Gluten, the main storage protein in wheat, barley, and rye, contains sequences rich in proline and glutamine that resist complete gastrointestinal degradation resulting in generation of immunogenic peptides. The peptides contain immunogenic epitopes that, following deamidation by tissue transglutaminase 2 (TG2), can be presented by HLA-DQ2/DQ8 molecules to gluten-specific CD4 + T cells, resulting in intestinal inflammation. This gluten-induced intestinal inflammation is known as celiac disease (CD) in susceptible individuals. A gluten-free diet (GFD) has been recognised as gold standard treatment to date, which requires lifelong strict compliance, therefore demanding alternative novel therapies. Fermented foods have emerged as promising reservoirs for selection of gluten-degrading probiotic strains as adjunctive therapeutic candidates. These strains may hydrolyse gluten and its immunogenic gluten peptides through specialised array of proteolytic enzymatic systems comprising endopeptidases, prolyl endopeptidases, aminopeptidases and dipeptidyl peptidases. This review critically examines the significance of gluten-degrading microorganisms with probiotic potential from fermented foods and their proteolytic enzyme system. Owing to their origin from fermented foods, the effect of fermentation parameters such as pH, strain selection, and substrate composition is also highlighted. The assessment of studies indicates that the fermentation mediated by selected gluten-degrading strains reduces the gluten content; however, these did not detoxify the immunogenic peptides completely. The potential strains support intestinal health through modulation of gut microbiota and attenuation of inflammatory responses which has been validated through in vitro and clinical studies, although their efficacy in managing CD remains unestablished. However, strain-specific differences, incomplete degradation of immunogenic peptides, and the lack of standardised protocols for evaluating gluten detoxification remain significant barriers to their application. Key points Fermented foods serve as a key reservoir for gluten-degrading microorganismsStrain-specific enzymes and fermentation conditions affect gluten hydrolysis.Clinical efficacy of potential strains has yet to be conclusively established.

works.title: Sensor-integrated PMMA bone cement enables multimodal data acquisition in a load-bearing orthopedic knee spacer implants
works.abstract: Introduction Periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) is a severe complication of total knee arthroplasty, is a leading cause of revision surgery, and is associated with significant morbidity. Two-stage exchange using antibiotic-loaded polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) spacers remains the clinical gold standard, yet the decision to reimplant relies largely on indirect markers and clinical judgment, as no method allows continuous in situ assessment of infection resolution. Here, we report the development of a sensorized knee spacer that transforms medical-grade PMMA bone cement from a passive structural material into an implantable multimodal sensing platform by embedding fully functional sensing and communication systems. Methods We developed an integration strategy addressing previously limiting factors, including exothermic polymerization, mechanical load transfer, and spatial constraints, while retaining the conventional PMMA molding principle during final spacer fabrication. A miniaturized multimodal sensor unit was integrated within PMMA cement, and the functionality of the embedded camera, spectrometer, positioning, and temperature sensors following cement integration was evaluated. The mechanical behavior of the sensor-integrated spacer was assessed under adapted dynamic biomechanical loading conditions based on ISO 14879-1:2020. In vivo functionality and longitudinal multimodal data acquisition were evaluated in a porcine pilot experiment using human knee spacer dimensions. Results Stable integration of the miniaturized multimodal sensor unit within PMMA cement was achieved while maintaining sensor functionality and wireless data transmission despite the thermal, mechanical, and geometric constraints of bone cement integration. The functionality of the embedded camera, spectrometer, positioning, and temperature sensors was maintained following cement integration. In vivo functionality and longitudinal multimodal data acquisition were demonstrated over 148 h in the porcine pilot experiment. Discussion These findings demonstrate the technical feasibility of integrating active sensing systems into load-bearing bone-cement implants under the investigated experimental conditions. The SmartSpacer provides a platform for longitudinal multimodal data acquisition during the spacer interval, establishing a technical basis for future studies investigating infection-associated biomarkers.

works.title: Drug-induced gastrointestinal toxicity: from pathophysiological mechanisms to human-relevant preclinical models
works.abstract: Drug-induced gastrointestinal toxicity (DiGIT) represents a major dose-limiting adverse effect that severely compromises patient outcomes and therapeutic efficacy across global populations. Frequently triggered by chemotherapeutic agents and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), DiGIT spans a clinical spectrum from mild dyspepsia to life-threatening complications, including severe mucositis, ulceration, and gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding. Because the GI tract serves as a primary site of drug exposure, its rapidly proliferating epithelial architecture, mucosal immune interface, and complex microbiota, essential components of intestinal homeostasis, are particularly susceptible to off-target therapeutic damage. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of DiGIT across the upper and lower GI tracts, examining the distinct toxicity profiles of NSAIDs and chemotherapy. We detail the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms, focusing on drug-induced epithelial damage, innate immune system activation, and microbiome dysbiosis, alongside current supportive management strategies. Finally, we highlight the preclinical landscape of in vitro toxicity testing, outlining how emerging, physiologically representative bioengineered models can better evaluate GI safety, streamline risk assessment, and improve candidate drug success.

works.title: Establishment of a robot-assisted ex vivo active shoulder simulator
works.abstract: Background Stable, repeatable, muscle-driven shoulder simulation remains difficult to achieve ex vivo , although it is essential for studying clinically relevant variables such as joint reaction forces, glenohumeral translations, and joint torques that cannot be measured directly during dynamic motion in vivo . Methods A robot-assisted active shoulder simulator (RAASS) was developed in which six cable-driven actuators applied forces to the rotator cuff and deltoid muscle group. An industrial robot maintained defined boundary conditions and recorded synchronized kinetic and kinematic data during active scapular-plane glenohumeral abduction in 19 fresh-frozen cadaveric shoulders. Closed-loop force control was used to regulate actuator loading. Internal rotation and horizontal adduction were constrained to 0°. Translational force targets maintained joint compression while muscle force ratios were updated across the range of motion. Results Active glenohumeral abduction to 60° was successfully reproduced in all specimens. The robot compensated for emerging torques and external loads, allowing the muscle actuators to remain the primary drivers of motion. Mean total muscle force increased significantly with abduction angle, from 81 ± 36 N/kg at 20° to 107 ± 28 N/kg at 60°. Superior translation increased significantly with abduction, whereas posterior and medial translations showed no significant angle-dependent changes. Horizontal adduction torque increased from 20° to 40° and remained elevated at 60°, and internal rotation torque reached its greatest magnitude at 40°. Conclusion This study demonstrates the feasibility of a robot-assisted ex vivo active shoulder simulator that combines muscle-driven motion with robotic load and constraint management. Beyond enabling controlled active abduction, the framework provides continuous, synchronized measurement of muscle forces, translations, torques, and kinematics. It allows the robot to serve as an active load-application and compensation interface. This represents a methodological advance for investigating shoulder stability, joint loading, and more complex dynamic shoulder motions.

works.title: Biomechanical analysis of pneumothorax: tissue failure, computational simulation, and clinical translation
works.abstract: From a biomechanical perspective, the development and persistence of pneumothorax are closely associated with damage to or functional failure of tissue structures responsible for maintaining pleural-cavity airtightness and pressure coupling. This review aims to summarize advances in the understanding of the mechanical mechanisms and computational modeling of pneumothorax development, lung collapse, and re-expansion, and to evaluate their potential for clinical translation. Three conceptual modes of tissue failure are outlined: stress-driven, material-driven, and overload-driven failure. The review also discusses the applications of hyperelastic, viscoelastic, and poroelastic constitutive models, as well as computational methods, including cohesive zone models (CZMs), the extended finite element method (XFEM), finite element analysis (FEA), and fluid–structure interaction (FSI) modeling. Current research remains constrained by insufficient characterization of material properties, limited representation of tissue heterogeneity, and inadequate experimental and clinical validation. These limitations reduce the comparability of model predictions and hinder their application to individualized clinical management. At present, these models are primarily used to elucidate biomechanical mechanisms and compare tissue responses under different conditions. Their practical utility in risk assessment, surgical planning, and optimization of drainage strategies requires further validation. Future research should prioritize the measurement of material properties, patient-specific model development, and rigorous experimental and clinical validation to provide a more reliable quantitative basis for mechanistic investigations and clinical decision-making in pneumothorax.

works.title: Mechanisms and translational strategies for extrahepatic bile duct regeneration: a review
works.abstract: Extrahepatic bile duct (EHBD) injury remains a major challenge in hepatobiliary medicine, because effective repair requires sustained epithelial integrity, structural continuity, and luminal patency. In this narrative review, we examine the biological basis of EHBD regeneration, focusing on cholangiocytes, peribiliary glands and the surrounding stromal microenvironment. We highlight redox regulation and tissue mechanics, along with signaling pathways that influence epithelial proliferation and fibrotic remodeling. We also compare regenerative strategies by intended application, including cell-based approaches for epithelial restoration, scaffolds for structural reconstruction, and pharmacological interventions to modify injury and repair. However, current evidence remains predominantly experimental, with limited clinical validation. Future translation will require functional epithelial recovery and sustained patency beyond scaffold degradation or withdrawal of temporary support, together with reproducible manufacturing and safety assessment.

works.title: Biotribology of meniscus degeneration: correlations between frictional, structural and compressive properties
works.abstract: Introduction Despite extensive knowledge of how degeneration-related structural changes affect the compressive properties of the meniscus, the associated tribological changes remain poorly understood. Moreover, both functionalities have largely been investigated independently, leaving a knowledge gap regarding possible interrelationships. The aim of this study was to elucidate how alterations in meniscus biomechanical and structural properties affect the tissues tribological properties. Methods Human menisci with varying degrees of degeneration were collected from patients undergoing total knee replacement surgery. The compressive meniscus properties were determined using established indentation and compression tests, while the tribological properties were analyzed under simulated gait conditions. Macroscopic as well as microscopic degeneration was assessed by means of Pauli scoring and quantitative histology of glycosaminoglycan, collagen and proteoglycan-4 content. Statistically, linear mixed model analysis and Spearman correlation were applied. Results Higher macroscopic degeneration severity was associated with both increased friction (ρ = 0.30–0.32, p < 0.05) and reduced compressive stiffness (ρ = 0.30, p < 0.05). Increased friction coefficients were significantly associated with lower initial elastic properties (ρ = 0.30–0.42, p < 0.05) and higher viscoelastic relaxation behavior (ρ = 0.30–0.35, p < 0.05). Discussion Degenerative changes in the meniscus manifest themselves in a coupled tribological-functional impairment. The interaction between altered friction and compressive properties could represent a mutually reinforcing, degeneration-promoting feedback loop. To prevent a potential function-driven vicious cycle, disease modifying therapies may target the meniscus’ dual functionality in gonarthrosis progression.

works.title: T cell mechanomemory takes training: cell-secreted factors reinforce short-term mechanosensing into long-term proliferation
works.abstract: Biomaterials provide a powerful tool for directing the function of T cells with applications from fundamental immunology research to immunotherapy. Intriguingly, controlling the mechanical stiffness of biomaterials used to activate T cells modulates a range of subsequent functions from early activation to differentiation. However, it is not fully understood whether the effect of initial, short-term mechanosensing is limited to immediate impacts on cell function or imparts a long-lasting imprint on cell function. This report demonstrates such a mechanomemory in the context of expansion; T cells activated on mechanically soft surfaces exhibit an extended proliferative phase for multiple generations following removal from the substrate. This effect results from a combination of cell-intrinsic changes and extrinsic factors associated with cell-cell signaling. Specifically, activation using a soft elastomer substrate extends subsequent proliferation over multiple cell divisions. This programming can initially be modified by extrinsic soluble factors secreted into the media; the conditioned media carries information about early mechanosensitive activation, as demonstrated using media exchange experiments. Notably, the impact of extrinsic factors on proliferation decreases over the course of expansion, showing that reinforcement of mechanosensing leads to establishment of mechanomemory. Together, these results suggest that populations of T cells can be trained to retain the mechanical imprint of an activating surface through continued reinforcement, potentially directing later function in a range of immunotherapy applications.

works.title: KDELR2 promotes the progression of non-small cell lung cancer by regulating HIF-1α mediated glycolysis
works.abstract: Introduction Across the world, lung cancer remains the foremost cause of death attributed to cancer, contributing to nearly one in five of cancer deaths. As the main histological form, non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) constitutes roughly 80%–85% of total diagnosed lung cancer cases. Patients diagnosed with advanced NSCLC have a 5-year survival rate lower than 20%, and persistent problem of drug resistance underscores the importance of developing new safe and efficacious drugs and exploring innovative therapeutic targets. The Lys-Asp-Glu-Leu (KDEL) endoplasmic reticulum (ER) protein retention receptors (KDELRs) is one of the earliest discovered intracellular transport receptors and essential for preserving the integrity of the early secretory pathway. Evidence indicates that KDELR2 facilitates the invasion and migration of NSCLC, although the fundamental mechanisms behind this remain poorly understood. The research suggestes that KDELR2 could enhance abilities of proliferation, migration, and invasion of NSCLC through hypoxia-inducible factor 1α (HIF-1α) dependent glycolytic metabolism and identified KDELR2 as a potential molecular target for the novel drug pseudoginsenoside Rh2 (P-G-Rh2), thereby offering a new therapeutic target and a potentially effective treatment agent for NSCLC. Methods The levels of KDELR2 were measured through real-time fluorescence quantitative PCR (RT‐qPCR), western blot, and immunohistochemistry (IHC). In vitro assays were carried out to evaluate impact of KDELR2 on functions of NSCLC cells and explore the underlying mechanism through cell counting kit‐8 (CCK‐8), western blot, transwell assays, and wound healing. Additionally, nude mice xenograft models were conducted for validating role of P‐G‐Rh2 in suppressing progression of NSCLC. Results KDELR2 expression is upregulated in NSCLC tissues, and its increased levels enhance the proliferation, invasion, and metastasis of NSCLC. Mechanistic studies indicate that KDELR2 drives progression of NSCLC by elevating HIF‐1α and subsequently activating glycolysis. Additionally, KDELR2 is recognized as a potential molecular target of P‐G‐Rh2. Further investigation reveals that P‐G‐Rh2 suppresses progression of NSCLC through by regulating the KDELR2/HIF‐1α/glycolysis axis. Conclusion KDELR2 promotes the progression of NSCLC via HIF‐1α-mediated glycolysis. Therefore, targeting the KDELR2/HIF-1α/glycolysis signaling pathway may become an effective therapeutic strategy for NSCLC. Meanwhile, KDELR2 is a potential molecular target of P‐G‐Rh2, indicating that P‐G‐Rh2 represents a promising novel therapeutic approach for NSCLC.

works.title: Continuous Capture of Recombinant Adeno‐Associated Virus Particles Using Twin‐Column CaptureSMB
works.abstract: Recombinant adeno-associated viruses (rAAVs) have gained increasing importance in gene therapy due to their safe and precise gene delivery. However, certain indications require substantially higher vector doses, pushing manufacturing capacity and cost of goods (COG) to its limits. In this study, we present a proof-of-concept evaluation of a continuous twin-column capture process (CaptureSMB) enabling direct purification of rAAV5 from minimally processed, nonlysed perfusion harvest without prior enzymatic nuclease digestion, concentration or buffer exchange.
