works.title: Systematic Evaluation of Cyanidioschyzon merolae Across Photobioreactor Systems: Linking Reactor Design to Biomass Production and Biochemical Composition
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Extremophilic red microalgae are promising platforms for sustainable biotechnology, combining robust growth under selective thermoacidophilic conditions with production of thermostable phycobiliproteins and carbon‐rich biomass. However, reactor‐dependent effects on growth, product formation, and biomass composition remain insufficiently resolved. Here, we systematically evaluated the extremophilic red microalga Cyanidioschyzon merolae across cultivation scales and reactor formats and benchmarked its performance against the well‐established Galdieria javensis and Limnospira platensis . In small‐scale multi‐cultivator photobioreactors and microfluidic growth chambers, C. merolae showed superior growth, reaching a maximum growth rate of 0.034 ± 0.001 h −1 and 8.3 ± 0.3 g L −1 cell dry weight. Microfluidic cultivation enabled growth analysis at single‐cell resolution and matched growth rates obtained in photobioreactors. To identify scalable production strategies, C. merolae was further cultivated in a flat‐panel photobioreactor (FPR) and a custom‐designed internally illuminated photobioreactor (IIPBR). The custom‐designed photobioreactor delivered the highest biomass concentration and productivity, yielding 11.5 ± 0.6 g L −1 cell dry weight and 1.07 ± 0.06 g L −1 d −1 , and comparable yields with regard to R‐phycocyanin and R‐allophycocyanin (R‐APC). Biomass analysis revealed substantial carbon and nitrogen contents, starch accumulation up to > 20% of cell dry weight, and fatty acids dominated by palmitic, linoleic, and oleic acids. Despite its reduced cell wall fraction, C. merolae contained structurally diverse, cultivation‐dependent polysaccharides. These results establish C. merolae as a versatile chassis for thermostable pigment production and renewable feedstock generation, highlighting photobioreactor design as a key determinant of productivity and biomass quality.

works.title: High Hydrogen Yields During Continuous Photofermentative Valorization of Hydrothermal Carbonization Process Water by Engineered Rhodobacter capsulatus
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Photofermentative hydrogen (H 2 ) production by purple non‐sulphur bacteria (PNSB) is a promising route for sustainable energy generation, although large‐scale application remains limited by substrate costs and process stability. Here, we demonstrate sustained H 2 production using an H 2 ‐overproducing Rhodobacter capsulatus Δ hupAB mutant cultivated on process water (PW) derived from the hydrothermal carbonization of food waste. Batch assays showed that buffered PW supports phototrophic growth, soluble chemical oxygen demand (COD) removal, and H 2 production without requiring defined carbon sources. Based on these results, continuous photofermentation was operated at a hydraulic retention time of 3.5 days using diluted PW supplemented only with phosphate buffer, operating for more than 600 h, with sustained COD removal and H 2 production. Average H 2 yields reached 178 mL H 2 g −1 COD during the stable operational period (100–350 h), comparing favourably with literature values. Carbon partitioning analyses revealed lower inorganic carbon formation under PW feeding, consistent with a redistribution of reducing equivalents towards nitrogenase activity. This behaviour was associated with lower biomass yields and enhanced H 2 production. Minimal CO 2 formation resulted in an almost pure H 2 stream. These results demonstrate the feasibility of continuous photofermentative valorization of PW for coupling waste valorization with high‐purity biohydrogen production.

works.title: Unravelling the Chemolithoautotrophic Metabolism of the Carboxydotrophic Knallgas Bacterium Hydrogenophaga pseudoflava
works.abstract: ABSTRACT The sustainable production of chemicals is critical to reducing greenhouse gas emissions and environmental pollution. Gaseous feedstocks from industrial waste streams and waste gasification, including CO, CO 2 and H 2 , represent abundant and underutilized resources for biotechnology. Syngas fermentation has been predominantly studied under anaerobic conditions, whereas aerobic processes may offer advantages for the biosynthesis of energy‐intensive products. One promising organism is the aerobic carboxydotroph Hydrogenophaga pseudoflava DSM 1084, whose chemolithoautotrophic metabolism remains poorly understood. To address this, we performed proteome analysis under different growth conditions and characterized deletion mutants of key enzymes involved in CO and H 2 oxidation. Deletion mutants showed that only CO dehydrogenase I and the membrane‐bound hydrogenase are essential for CO and H 2 oxidation, respectively. The role of the putative second CO dehydrogenase remains to be elucidated, and the soluble hydrogenase may contribute to redox balancing under microaerobic or anaerobic conditions. In addition, the H 2 ‐sensing regulatory system appears to be nonfunctional, and the transhydrogenase PntAB supports redox homeostasis during chemolithoautotrophic growth. Electrons from CO or H 2 are transferred via the reduced quinone pool to NADH through proton‐motive force‐driven reverse electron transfer. Nevertheless, growth on CO remains slower than on CO 2 /H 2 . In contrast to CO 2 /H 2 , an unphysiologically high CO concentration (80%) led to a major proteome rearrangement, with 1879 of 3640 reliably quantified proteins showing altered abundance compared to fructose‐grown cells, including a pronounced stress response. Under such conditions, cells are likely to invest additional energy to maintain redox balance. Together with the less energy‐conserving autotrophic branch of the respiratory chain and cytoplasmic CO oxidation, this results in inefficient CO conversion and reduced growth.

works.title: The Arms Race Between Bacteria and Their Viruses: Update on Phage Countermeasures Against Bacterial Defence Systems
works.abstract: ABSTRACT In this editorial, I summarize recent progress on phage‐encoded anti‐defence against bacterial anti‐phage systems (APS). Computational approaches based on structural predictions of co‐folding bacterial and phage proteins identified many new PAD sponge proteins. New anti‐CRISPR‐Cas systems were characterized that destroy cas12a mRNA, inactivate Cas12a by acetylation, engage the seed region of the crRNA, or prevent Cas3 from cleaving DNA. The phage defence protein Gad1 forms an octamer web that wraps around the complex of the Gabija APS. Tad1 and 2 are phage sponge proteins that sequester signalling nucleotides of the Thoeris APS. Tad3 to 7 interact directly with the ThsB sensor and Tad8 with the ThsA effector of the Thoeris APS. Phage sponge proteins were also described inactivating the CBASS and Pycsar APS. Still other phages use phosphodiesterases that cleave cyclic nucleotide signals to inactivate APS. Many bacterial APS effectors are NADase, destroying the essential metabolite NAD + . Phages evolved enzymes that resynthesize NAD + from its cleavage products or proteins directly inactivating the NADase. Many phages degrade the bacterial genome which creates signals activating the Metis or the Kongming APS. Phages counteracted these APS by suppressing pathways leading to the creation of particular mononucleotides degradation products detected by these APS. Several APS cleave specific tRNA, phages responded by mutating cleavage sites in tRNA (anti‐PARIS) or increasing tRNA expression to compensate for their destruction (anti‐Septu). Phages counteract toxin‐antitoxin APS by evolving their own antitoxin or by blocking the toxin protein. Researchers described cases where phages escaped detection by mutating phage proteins detected by bacterial sensors. Against the stringent response phages responded by destroying alarmones or inactivating enzymes producing these stress signals. The arms race between bacteria and phages can involve complicated layers of defence and anti‐defences and both bacteria and phages encode multiple defence systems.

works.title: Integrated Microbial Profiling Identifies Bacterial and Fungal Communities in Pseudomyxoma Peritonei Mucin
works.abstract: Pseudomyxoma peritonei (PMP) is a rare mucinous malignancy in which tumour-associated microbial communities remain poorly characterised, particularly, their fungal component and spatial organisation. We applied an integrated workflow combining 16S and 18S rRNA gene sequencing, microbial culture, histochemical staining, chromogenic RNAscope in situ hybridisation and a patient-derived xenograft model to investigate bacterial and fungal communities in control tissues and low- and high-grade PMP mucin. Bacterial and fungal DNA was detected in PMP-associated mucin, with grade-associated differences in bacterial composition and predicted functional potential. Viable bacteria were recovered from human PMP samples and xenograft-derived mucin. Fungal structures were independently supported by periodic acid-Schiff and Calcofluor White staining, while RNAscope localised bacterial 16S and fungal 18S rRNA signals within epithelial and mucin-rich tumour regions. Comparable microbial signals were observed in the xenograft model. Together, these complementary approaches identify PMP mucin as a multi-kingdom microbial niche and provide the first characterisation of its associated mycobiome. This integrated analytical framework may facilitate the investigation of microorganisms in other low-biomass, mucin-rich tumour environments and provides a basis for future mechanistic studies of microbe-host interactions in PMP.

works.title: Genetic Engineering Efforts to Generate Chlamydomonas Strains for Large‐Scale Biomolecule Production
works.abstract: Chlamydomonas reinhardtii is an established model microalga. Its easy manipulation, metabolic flexibility and tractable genomes allowed researchers to investigate fundamental processes such as photosynthesis using genetic studies for decades. Chlamydomonas is not naturally rich in lipids or pigments compared to industrially relevant microalgae. However, we highlight how its biotechnological potential relies on advanced genetic and metabolic engineering strategies, now possible due to the availability of extensive toolbox and synthetic biology platforms, which can improve industrial traits and allow to produce a variety of biomolecules of biotechnological interest. We provide examples of biomolecule production (terpenoids and recombinant proteins), and show that productivities (mg/L) are in the same range or could even be higher than those reached in other photosynthetic chassis (e.g., cyanobacteria or mosses). We point out that despite these achievements, the industrial implementation of C. reinhardtii is still lacking. Further technological advancements as well as clear international regulations and social acceptance are fundamental to reach the full potential of this microalga.

works.title: Reprogramming Native Cryptic Plasmids Enables Antibiotic‐Selection‐Free Urate Degradation by Escherichia coli Nissle 1917
works.abstract: Hyperuricemia is associated with renal injury and disturbances in gut microbial ecology. Intestinal urate clearance by engineered probiotics is limited by antibiotic-free functional maintenance and the oxygen requirement of urate oxidase (UOX). We reprogrammed the native cryptic plasmids of Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN) to construct M12U, a marker-free dual-plasmid strain. pMUT2 carried an HucR-regulated urate-responsive UOX module, while pMUT1 encoded a low-oxygen-responsive UOX module and Tat-targeted Vitreoscilla haemoglobin (tat-VHB). M12U degraded urate in vitro and retained activity under low-oxygen conditions. In hyperuricemic mice (n = 5 per group), oral M12U reduced serum urate, creatinine, blood urea nitrogen, inflammatory cytokines and renal histopathological injury. 16S rRNA profiling showed increased microbial richness and a partial shift in community composition toward healthy controls. Shotgun metagenomics revealed enrichment of Lactobacillus johnsonii and Bacteroides acidifaciens, together with increased metabolic potential related to the pentose phosphate pathway and glutathione metabolism. Faecal metabolomics showed reduced uric acid abundance and increased thiamine monophosphate and argininosuccinic acid. These results support further evaluation of dual-native-plasmid architectures for gut-directed urate clearance.

works.title: Correction to ‘Eco‐Microbiology: A Frugal‐Circular Framework for Biosafe, Low‐Cost Practical Microbiology in Secondary Education’
Biofilm Engineering for Efficient Substrate‐Enzyme Interactions to Enhance Enzymatic PET Degradation
works.abstract: Despite extensive protein engineering efforts to significantly increase the catalytic efficiency of plastic-degrading enzymes, inefficient plastic-enzyme interactions during the interfacial biocatalytic process continue to impede their widespread applications. Here, we engineered the complete csgBACEFG curli operon through multicopy chromosomal integration to generate a csgBACEFG-optimized (CSGO) biofilm with enhanced curli assembly and plastic-surface adhesion. Unlike previou curli-based enzyme immobilization studies using individual CsgA curli components or pre-existing curli scaffolds, our strategy uses the complete curli assembly machinery to construct a dense, surface-associated catalytic biofilm. FAST-PETase was then embedded in a 2-day PET-surface CSGO biofilm through the SpyTag/SpyCatcher system, producing 2.5-fold more hydrolysis products from PET film depolymerization than soluble FAST-PETase with the same initial enzyme mass. The carrier-free biofilm-supported FAST-PETase also retained more than 50% of its first-cycle product formation after five 24-h PET nanoplastic (NanoPET) degradation cycles. These findings support biofilm-mediated enhancement of PET depolymerization and provide a proof-of-concept strategy that may inform future biofilm-assisted plastic treatment.

works.title: Correction to ‘ Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG and Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis BB ‐12 Promote Infected Wound Healing via Regulation of the Wound Microenvironment’
works.abstract: Yin, Z., Y. Wang, X. Feng, et al. 2024. “ Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG and Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis BB-12 Promote Infected Wound Healing via Regulation of the Wound Microenvironment.” Microbial Biotechnology 17: e70031. https://doi.org/10.1111/1751-7915.70031. Following a careful post-publication review of our original experimental datasets, we identified an error in Figure 2B. Specifically, the representative wound image for the Control group at Day 1 was inadvertently duplicated with the corresponding image from the BB-12 group. We have re-examined all original experimental records and image archives, and the correct representative image for the Control group at Day 1 has been identified and verified. Accordingly, Figure 2 has been revised to ensure the accurate presentation of all experimental groups. We confirm that this correction does not affect the quantitative analyses, results, interpretation, or conclusions of the study. We apologize for this error.

works.title: Riboflavin Metabolism Links Metabolic State to Biofilm Development, Cell‐Envelope Homeostasis, and Antimicrobial Susceptibility in Mycobacterium tuberculosis
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Biofilm formation and phenotypic drug tolerance contribute to the persistence and treatment challenges associated with Mycobacterium tuberculosis ( M. tb ). Although M. tb lacks canonical quorum‐sensing systems, it exhibits coordinated metabolic and cell‐envelope adaptations during biofilm development, suggesting the existence of alternative mechanisms linking cellular metabolism to multicellular behaviour. Here, using a combination of functional genomics, metabolic perturbation and systems‐level analyses, we identify riboflavin metabolism as a regulatory axis influencing biofilm development and antimicrobial susceptibility in M. tb . CRISPRi‐mediated knockdown and targeted overexpression of riboflavin biosynthetic genes markedly altered biofilm architecture, cell morphology, envelope ultrastructure, membrane permeability and lipid composition, with ribA2 and ribF emerging as potential metabolic vulnerabilities. Exogenous riboflavin enhanced biofilm formation, whereas the riboflavin antimetabolite roseoflavin suppressed this phenotype. Notably, cell‐free supernatants from late‐stage cultures, accumulated higher levels of riboflavin and restored biofilm formation in a riboflavin‐biosynthesis‐deficient strain, supporting a diffusible regulatory function beyond the established metabolic roles of riboflavin‐derived FMN and FAD. Integrated transcriptomic and lipidomic analyses revealed coordinated reprogramming of biofilm‐associated regulatory pathways, cell‐envelope lipid metabolism and the F 420 biosynthetic network, accompanied by increased susceptibility to anti‐tuberculosis drugs. Molecular docking further identified potential interactions of riboflavin with regulatory proteins associated with biofilm and stress‐response pathways. Together, these findings establish riboflavin metabolism as a previously underappreciated regulatory layer connecting microbial metabolism, biofilm development, cell‐envelope homeostasis and drug tolerance. This metabolic axis provides a potential framework for developing microbial biotechnology‐based strategies to interfere with biofilm‐associated persistence and improve the efficacy of anti‐tuberculosis therapeutics.

works.title: Succession of Microbial Communities and Identification of Indigenous PAH‐Tolerant Bacteria Under Multiple PAH Stresses in Mangrove Sediments From Maowei Sea, Guangxi, China
works.abstract: Elucidating microbial community shifts under polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) stress and screening indigenous PAH-tolerant microbial resources are valuable for exploring potential bioremediation strategies for PAH-contaminated mangrove ecosystems. In this study, surface sediments were collected from mangrove wetlands of the Maowei Sea, Guangxi, China. Three rounds of successive 7-day enrichment cultures were performed with gradually elevated PAH concentrations using phenanthrene, anthracene, and pyrene as target carbon substrates, followed by isolation and taxonomic identification of PAH-adapted bacteria. The results demonstrated that microbial community diversity decreased with increasing enrichment rounds and varied significantly among different PAH substrate treatments. ANOSIM confirmed significant differences in community structure across enrichment cycles and PAH treatments (p < 0.01), consistent with the ordination patterns revealed by Non-metric Multidimensional Scaling (NMDS). The PAH-adapted microbial communities were predominantly dominated by Pseudomonadota (33.2%-99.9%), Bacillota (0%-48.3%), and Actinomycetota (0.1%-33.7%). In total, 17 indigenous PAH-tolerant bacterial strains belonging to eight genera within the phylum Pseudomonadota were isolated, with representative strains affiliated with Labrys, Sphingomonas, and Acinetobacter. Within the tested physiological gradient ranges, Labrys sp. F3-1 and Acinetobacter sp. B1-5 exhibited optimal growth at pH 5.0, 40°C, and 15‰ salinity, while Sphingomonas sp. N2-15 showed the best growth performance at pH 5.0, 25°C, and 4‰ salinity. Growth assays under PAH pressure further verified that these three isolates could survive and proliferate in PAH-amended selective media under the tested laboratory conditions. This study provides indigenous PAH-tolerant bacterial resources and fundamental community-level insights for future investigations on microbial-based remediation of PAH-polluted mangrove sediments. Notably, the high PAH concentrations applied during laboratory enrichment (100-500 mg/L) were substantially higher than in situ environmental levels; the observed microbial responses and strain physiological traits reflect adaptive characteristics under extreme laboratory selective pressure and should be cautiously extrapolated to natural mangrove ecosystems.

works.title: A scalable whole-cell biocatalytic process for food-compatible production of resolvin D5 using the edible mushroom Pleurotus ostreatus
works.abstract: Specialized pro-resolving mediators (SPMs) actively promote the resolution of inflammation, but their scalable and food-compatible production remains challenging because current methods rely on multistep chemical synthesis, mammalian cells, purified enzymes, crude enzyme preparations, or recombinant microorganisms. Here, we developed a scalable, food-compatible submerged-cultured whole-cell biocatalytic process for the production of resolvin D5 (RvD5; 7S,17S-dihydroxydocosahexaenoic acid) from docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) using the edible mushroom Pleurotus ostreatus. Submerged-cultured P. ostreatus whole cells stereoselectively converted DHA to RvD5 via a 17S-hydroxydocosahexaenoic acid intermediate through an endogenous lipoxygenase (LOX)-mediated double-oxygenation pathway, without enzyme purification or heterologous gene expression. Optimization of submerged cultivation conditions (cultivation period and medium composition) increased RvD5 production by 2.1-fold, and subsequent optimization of whole-cell biotransformation parameters (temperature, pH, cell and substrate concentrations, polyvinylpyrrolidone and ethanol supplementation, reaction time, and agitation) resulted in an overall 13.4-fold increase relative to the initial conditions. Under the optimized flask-scale conditions, whole cells produced 2.14mM (0.77g/L) RvD5 from 2.5mM DHA with an 85.6% molar yield within 40min. The process was successfully scaled up to a 3.0-L stirred-tank bioreactor (1.0-L working volume), producing 2.08mM (0.75g/L) RvD5 with an 83.2% molar yield within 60min. The developed cultivation-based edible fungal whole-cell biocatalytic process integrates catalyst preparation, efficient RvD5 biosynthesis, and scalable bioprocessing, providing a practical strategy for the scalable biotechnological production of DHA-derived SPMs.

works.title: Science Does Not Run on Evidence Alone
works.abstract: Scientists take pride in producing knowledge and finding solutions. However, the impact and use they really have depend largely on something we rarely discuss in scientific journals: inspiration. Often, the ability to inspire is attributed to a few individuals with special talent. Looking at the evidence, this is hardly justified: psychological research describes inspiration as a defined and measurable construct with three characteristics - it is evoked, it is motivating, and it is transcendent. That it is evoked is the important part, because it means inspiration reaches a person from outside and somebody is supplying it. Therefore, here we argue that we can learn to do so and this is increasingly important. Inspiration is associated with the creativity and productivity of scientific work, with the success of scientific careers, and also with the way public opinion embraces scientific content and findings. So, what can we do? We suggest first of all measuring and counting inspiration, appreciating the work in which it actually happens, building a sense of belonging to and into science early, and most importantly: doing it ourselves.

works.title: A domain library approach for generating antibodies that recruit T-cells with enhanced cytotoxicity using new bispecific bivalent antibodies
works.abstract: Traditionally, enhancing the function of T cell-recruiting antibodies requires a labor-intensive two-step process: initial phage display screening for binding affinity and secondary screening for cytotoxic activity. In this study, we utilized the bispecific bivalent antibody framework 'BiBian' and combined VHH phage display with a domain library approach for the generation of antibodies that recruit T-cells, thereby facilitating this evolution. By leveraging the modular nature of the single-domain component, we bypassed the affinity pre-selection phase by directly grafting mutant VHH libraries onto the BiBian framework for immediate cytotoxicity screening. While conventional methods were limited to evaluating only six candidates for cytotoxicity out of 264 initial clones, this method enabled the direct functional assessment of all 264 clones. This comprehensive approach significantly reduced the risk of overlooking high-potency variants that may not exhibit a linear correlation between binding affinity and functional output. Ultimately, three antibodies identified via this method exhibited a lower IC 50 for cytotoxic activity (down to 0.05 nM) than the top-performing candidate obtained through traditional methods (0.30 nM). In this proof-of-concept study, this accelerated functional-first strategy enabled the rapid evaluation of candidate potency within the target bivalent format. While further validation across other targets and antibody formats will be required to confirm broader applicability, these findings highlight the potential of the Dolag-ArT strategy for direct functional screening.

works.title: Predicting Achievable Carboxylic Acid and Amino Acid Titers
works.abstract: Industrial fermentation offers a promising route to produce enantiopure, bio-based carboxylic acids and amino acids. To identify the techno-economic and environmental sustainability of biotechnological production routes, early-stage process design and assessment are generally performed. For industrial-scale sustainability, achieving a high product concentration (titer) is critical. However, methods for predicting achievable acid fermentation titers are constrained by a lack of both ex-ante correlations and industrial-scale data. Therefore, we introduce a novel method to estimate the achievable titer for carboxylic acids and amino acids, based solely on the pH-corrected hydrophobicity (log D o/w , derived from log P o/w and p K a ), irrespective of the microorganism used. By analyzing 58 high, literature-reported, titers for carboxylates and amino acids, we formulated a 3-parameter logistic upper-bound function that describes this hydrophobicity-titer relationship (asymptote: 205 ± 21 g L -1 , N = 23). The function describes an upper boundary for optimised processes rather than an expected titer for arbitrary conditions. This function was applied to estimate the achievable titers of malonic acid, glycolic acid, cis,cis ‑muconic acid, and butyric acid reaching up to 204, 204, 200, and 172 g L⁻¹ at pH 7 respectively, while their expected titer decreases to approximately 164, 163, 73, and 31 g L⁻¹ at pH 3. Literature titers for the same product and microorganism at two pH values confirm this direction. The empirical correlation obtained in this study enables rapid, physics-informed estimation of achievable acid fermentation titers. Therefore, this method supports more reliable ex-ante bioprocess assessment and may accelerate sustainable bio-based acid production.

works.title: Cooperative mutations reshape lid dynamics in thermophilic lipase LipT6 enhancing stability and biodiesel production
works.abstract: Enzymatic biodiesel production offers a sustainable alternative to chemical transesterification, but industrial application of lipases is limited by acidic pH and high alcohol concentrations. Here, we combined previously identified stabilizing mutations in the thermophilic lipase LipT6 from Geobacillus stearothermophilus T6 to generate the S5 variant (H86Y/E251C/A269T/G332C/R374W) and investigated the molecular basis of its improved performance. S5 retained 94% of its activity after 1h at pH 4.8, compared with 33% for wild-type LipT6, and increased conversion of waste chicken oil to fatty acid methyl esters from 30.4% to 71.3%. The variant also showed increased thermal stability under neutral, acidic, and ethanol-rich conditions. Its determined 2.4Å crystal structure closely matched the wild-type closed-lid conformation, with a Cα RMSD of 0.38Å, indicating that enhanced function did not result from major structural rearrangements. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed conformation-dependent effects: wild-type and S5 behaved similarly in the closed state, whereas S5 exhibited greater lid flexibility and broader conformational sampling in the open state. Back-to-wild-type reversions in silico produced distinct shifts in lid sampling, supporting a cooperative contribution of the engineered mutations. Structural analysis further suggested that H86Y alters the environment of the Zn²⁺-binding region and adjacent lid hinge, while core mutations provide complementary stabilization. These findings demonstrate that cooperative engineering of core stability and lid dynamics can improve lipase performance under biodiesel-relevant conditions.

works.title: Application of bivalve shells for the removal of trace levels of micropollutants from wastewater under continuous flow conditions
Liquid‐Suspendable Metabolic Sensors Allow Real‐Time Oxygen Consumption Monitoring in Caco‐2 and Colon Organoid‐Based Gut‐on‐a‐Chip Models
works.abstract: The organ-on-a-chip field is a rapidly evolving area of expertise, combining enhanced physiological relevance with a wide range of functional readouts across diverse cellular models. One such readout is oxygen metabolism, which serves as a key indicator of mitochondrial function. In this study, we utilized metabolic sensors designed for real-time measurement of oxygen consumption, reflecting aerobic respiration, within a commercially available microfluidic platform. We demonstrated that time-resolved detection of oxygen consumption is feasible within the system's microliter-scale volumes and that chemically induced changes in cellular oxygen metabolism can be monitored in real time in two ready-to-use gut-on-a-chip models. In summary, this novel application of metabolic sensors enables direct evaluation of mitochondrial function in complex cellular environments by addressing key analytical challenges often encountered in organ-on-a-chip systems due to their limited size and structural complexity.

works.title: Redirecting Metabolic Flux to Minimize By‐Product Formation Enables Efficient De Novo Biosynthesis of Chlorogenic Acid in Escherichia coli
works.abstract: Chlorogenic acid (CGA) is an important natural hydroxycinnamic acid ester with diverse biological activities, including antioxidant, antibacterial, and potential antitumor properties. However, efficient microbial titer of CGA remains challenging because of insufficient hydroxylation efficiency, by-product accumulation, and limited host tolerance. Herein, an efficient and sustainable microbial platform for de novo CGA biosynthesis was constructed in Escherichia coli. Enhancement of the NAD(H) biosynthetic pathway increased intracellular reducing power and increased hydroxylation efficiency. A synergistic hydroxylation module consisting of the p-coumarate 3-hydroxylase from Saccharothrix espanaensis (SeC3H) and the flavin reductase from Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PaHpaC)was further introduced to promote the conversion of p-coumaric acid (pCA) to caffeic acid (CA) and redirect metabolic flux toward CGA biosynthesis. Rational engineering of 4-coumarate-CoA ligase from Arabidopsis thaliana (At4CL) increased substrate selectivity and decreased the formation of the major by-product p-coumaroylquinic acid (pCQA). In addition, transcriptomic analysis identified lsrG, a gene associated with the AI-2 quorum-sensing system, as a beneficial target whose overexpression further enhanced CGA titer. The final engineered strain produced 7220.3 mg/L CGA in a 50 L fed-batch fermentation. The strategies developed herein may provide an effective metabolic engineering framework for the sustainable biosynthesis of CGA and other aromatic natural products.

works.title: Improving aerobic fermentation performance of glucose to gluconic acid production by cooperating with Gluconobacter oxydans and diatoms
CultureBoost: an intelligent framework for retrospective analysis of commercial cell culture processes
Correction to: Integrated Serum Pharmacochemistry, Metabolomics, and Network Pharmacology to Reveal the Material Basis and Mechanism of Juan-tong-yin in the Treatment of Endometriosis
Mining and engineering of ω-transaminases for the biocatalytic synthesis of (R)-3-aminobutanol
Mechanisms of simultaneous removal of nitrate nitrogen and ofloxacin from water by microscale zero-valent iron/pyrite coupled with denitrifying microorganisms
Synergistic activation of peroxymonosulfate by Fe 3 O 4 /diatomite composite for efficient tetracycline degradation: mechanistic insights from experiments and density functional theory
works.abstract: Abstract BACKGROUND Tetracycline (TC) is a persistent antibiotic contaminant in water; because conventional treatments cannot adequately remove it, its persistence raises concerns about antibiotic resistance. To enhance degradation, magnetic Fe 3 O 4 /diatomite (DT) composites were synthesized via hydrothermal methods using natural porous DT to prevent the aggregation of Fe 3 O 4 nanoparticles and improve the reusability of the catalyst. RESULTS Characterization confirmed the successful Fe 3 O 4 loading onto DT with uniform elemental distribution, preserved pore structure, redox‐active Fe sites, and high thermal stability. The composite with 10% Fe 3 O 4 (10‐FDT) exhibited superior catalytic activity compared to Fe 3 O 4 or peroxymonosulfate alone. Under optimized conditions (25 mg L −1 TC, 0.20 g L−1 10‐FDT, 2.5 mmol L −1 peroxymonosulfate, pH 4), 87.4% TC degradation was achieved in 3 h. Degradation efficiency improved with catalyst and oxidant dosage, moderate acidity, and elevated temperature, but was inhibited by chloride ions and humic acid, while carbonate and dihydrogen phosphate ions enhanced the performance of the system. Radical quenching and electron spin resonance analyses revealed hydroxyl and sulfate radicals, alongside a dominant non‐radical singlet oxygen pathway linked to oxygen vacancies in DT. Density functional theory showed that electron transfer from DT to Fe 3 O 4 promotes oxidant adsorption and lowers the activation barriers for the formation of singlet oxygen. Mass spectrometry and molecular orbital analyses indicated TC degradation via functional group loss and ring opening. CONCLUSION The 10‐FDT composite proves to be an effective and stable catalyst for advanced oxidation processes, retaining 68.4% of its catalytic activity after three cycles and maintaining over 75% degradation efficiency in real wastewater samples. This highlights its strong potential for practical, scalable wastewater treatment applications. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry (SCI).

works.title: Covalent immobilization of urokinase onto glutaraldehyde-functionalized Fe₃O₄ magnetic nanoparticles for enhanced stability, reusability, and fibrinolytic performance
Challenges in meeting the mass transfer demands of high‐density perfusion cultures in single‐use bioreactors
works.abstract: Abstract Increasing protein therapeutics production by adopting intensified perfusion cultures places high demand on the mass transfer capabilities of single‐use bioreactors (SUB). Here, we compare these capabilities for four SUB designs against worst‐case O 2 transfer requirements for supporting Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) perfusion cultures. Impact of power dissipation, gas flow rate, O 2 enrichment, pCO 2 and sparge‐hole size on O 2 and CO 2 mass transfer (OTR and CTR) was characterized. Only one design delivered sufficient O 2 and removed sufficient CO 2 to support a worst‐case cell line at 100 × 10 6 viable cells/mL with a single‐sparger at both 50 and 1000 L scale. Larger‐scale versions of 3 designs were also tested. Performance at a 50‐L scale was not predictive of large‐scale performance (200 or 1000 L) for any design. Changes in the volume and composition of the gas phase during residence in the vessels were characterized. Substantial changes were found. Calculations of predicted culture pCO 2 were performed across the design space, assuming a respiratory quotient of 1. A response surface was constructed to predict culture pCO 2 and used to examine the consequences of various strategies for increasing OTR. Most strategies disproportionately increase OTR relative to CTR, leading to an increase in culture pCO 2 . The implications on SUB design and scale‐up for high‐intensity perfusion cultures are discussed.

works.title: Effects of relative humidity control on shrinkage, hardening thickness, and medicinal quality indicators of yam during hot air drying
Engineering a production platform for the potent antipseudomonal antibiotic mureidomycin A by reprogramming the pacidamycin biosynthetic gene cluster
works.abstract: BACKGROUND: Uridyl peptide antibiotics display potent activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a pathogen causing severe nosocomial infections. The four subclasses-mureidomycins, pacidamycins, napsamycins, and sansanmycins-inhibit the underexplored bacterial target phospho-MurNAc-pentapeptide translocase (MraY). Structurally, these compounds contain a 3'-deoxyuridine linked to a central diaminobutyric acid. The latter is situated within a pseudo tetra- or pentapeptide moiety, assembled by a non-ribosomal peptide synthetase machinery. The subclasses are distinguished by variations in the incorporated amino acids. Native producer strains typically synthesize numerous different uridyl peptide antibiotics in low yields. Since the pacidamycin gene cluster displays higher overall yields compared to the napsamycin cluster in identical expression systems, we aimed to reprogram it into a selective production platform for the highly bioactive mureidomycin A. This approach is intended to streamline isolation processes and support hit-to-lead optimization. RESULTS: Streptomyces albus J1074 was identified as the most promising host for heterologous expression of the pacidamycin gene cluster. Subsequently, media screening and precursor feeding were conducted, and regulators of closely related gene clusters were introduced into the heterologous host. The overexpression of the NpsM regulator of the napsamycin gene cluster increased production significantly. Next, the pacidamycin gene cluster was engineered to produce the more potent mureidomycins. Variable positions of the peptide moiety were individually targeted by domain or module swaps of the non-ribosomal peptide synthetase machinery. More specifically, these were replaced by homologs of the napsamycin gene cluster, resulting in strains mainly producing sansanmycin A or mureidomycin A. Promoter engineering enhanced mureidomycin A production in the final strain, correlating with increased transcription levels in RNA sequencing experiments on an intermediate strain harboring the same promoters. CONCLUSIONS: Hybrid uridyl peptide antibiotic gene clusters were constructed by genetically engineering the pacidamycin cluster, demonstrating the versatility of these clusters. While the native pacidamycin cluster only produced pacidamycin D and S, the final strain yields the more bioactive mureidomycin A and Met-pacidamycin 5. Additionally, sansanmycin A (syn. Met-pacidamycin 4) can be isolated from an intermediate construct of this study. This expands the access to different analogs and highlights further engineering potential, which will facilitate the future development of these promising antibiotics.

works.title: Identification of ferulic acid tolerance targets in engineered Komagataella phaffii by transcriptomics-integrated genome-scale metabolic modeling
works.abstract: Ferulic acid (FA) is an abundant aromatic precursor in lignocellulosic biomass and a promising substrate for vanillin biosynthesis, but its toxicity limits microbial conversion at elevated concentrations. Komagataella phaffii is a widely used non-conventional yeast cell factory with favorable properties for aromatic compound production, yet the cellular mechanisms underlying FA tolerance in this host remain poorly understood. An engineered K. phaffii strain carrying a heterologous FA-to-vanillin pathway was exposed to 20 mM FA under non-induced (FE–NI) and methanol-induced (FE-I) conditions. Both conditions exhibited higher growth rates and final cell densities compared with the wild-type, with FE-I exhibiting active FA catabolism and transient vanillin accumulation. Notably, FE–NI achieved comparable tolerance without detectable FA consumption, indicating that metabolic reprogramming of the host cell contributes to FA tolerance. Transcriptomic profiling revealed condition-dependent stress responses: FE–NI activated a host-level program comprising cell surface reinforcement, mitochondrial energy and redox support, and central carbon remodeling, whereas FE-I coupled active FA conversion with enhanced aldehyde detoxification and sugar-metabolism remodeling. Candidate tolerance targets were prioritized by integrating transcriptome data with a genome-scale metabolic model using an E-Flux approach. Functional validation by overexpression in the wild-type strain identified AGC1 and PAS_chr3_0834 as the most effective targets under non-induced and methanol-induced conditions, with colony number increasing 7.4-fold and 4.0-fold relative to the control, respectively. Co-expression of AGC1 and PAS_chr3_0834 increased biomass accumulation relative to the wild-type but did not exceed the effect of AGC1 alone under the tested condition. This study reveals condition-dependent FA tolerance programs in engineered K. phaffii and shows that integrating transcriptomics with genome-scale metabolic modeling can facilitate the identification of tolerance targets. The validated targets represent valuable engineering options for improving the robustness of K. phaffii cell factories employed in FA-based aromatic compound bioconversion.

works.title: Aspergillus terreus MAK153 against Fusarium oxysporum: biocontrol, metabolites, and simvastatin docking
works.abstract: This study demonstrates the considerable antagonistic activity of Aspergillus terreus MAK153 against a pathogenic Fusarium oxysporum AUMC3191 isolate. In dual culture assay, soil-isolated Aspergillus terreus Thom effectively hindered F. oxysporum AUMC3191 growth and impressively blocked zearalenone (ZEN) synthesis. Scanning electron microscopy demonstrated significant damage to F. oxysporum hyphae, such as abnormalities, shrinkage, bending, and deformity. Molecular identification through rDNA ITS sequence analysis confirmed the isolate as Aspergillus terreus, registered in GeneBank (Accession No. OR480103). GC/MS profiling of A. terreus MAK153 identified several bioactive secondary metabolites, notably estragole, caryophyllene, 2,4-di-tert-butylphenol, 1-docosene, 1-docosanol, olean-12-ene-3,28-diol, and simvastatin. Statistical analysis revealed a very strong positive correlation (r = 0.99) between chromatographic peak area% and peak area values. The influence of nutrient sources on simvastatin production was evaluated using four culture media. FTIR and HPLC analyses confirmed simvastatin biosynthesis, while HPLC revealed significant medium-dependent variation in yield (p < 0.001). Camellia sinensis Tea broth (CTB) elicited the highest yield, dominating extracellular filtrate accumulation (145.93 ± 1.13 mg/mL). Molecular docking simulations assessed simvastatin's binding affinity to HMG-CoA reductase and 3-ketosteroid reductase, yielding binding energies of -8.0 and -7.8 kcal/mol, respectively. The interactions involved multiple hydrophobic bonds and hydrogen bonds, suggesting simvastatin functions as a multi-target inhibitor capable of disrupting ergosterol biosynthesis at two distinct sites. Notably, this study represents the first computational exploration of simvastatin's interaction with 3-ketosteroid reductase, with implications for estrogen signalling modulation and potential therapeutic applications. KEY POINTS: • Aspergillus terreus MAK153 inhibits F. oxysporum growth and zearalenone production • Aspergillus terreus induces significant hyphal damage in F. oxysporum using SEM • Simvastatin-HMG-CoA and 3-ketosteroid interaction could modulate estrogen-related pathways potentially.

works.title: Next-generation precision fermentation: integrating engineered cell factories, bioprocess intensification, and smart bioprocessing
works.abstract: Precision fermentation (PF) uses engineered microbial cell factories to manufacture defined products under controlled bioprocess conditions. In this review, PF is treated operationally as the integration of engineered hosts with metabolic engineering and process control, while traditional food fermentations without engineered production strains are excluded. The field now spans pharmaceuticals, food ingredients, industrial enzymes, specialty chemicals, and biopolymers, but commercial translation remains constrained by biological non-linearity, substrate and feedstock variability, mass-transfer limitations at scale, downstream recovery, and the cost gap with incumbent processes. This mini-review examines five connected layers: engineered microbial chassis; design build test learn (DBTL) and multi-omics-guided metabolic engineering; bioreactor intensification; Process Analytical Technology (PAT), soft sensors and AI-enabled control; and techno-economic and life cycle assessment. Quantitative case studies illustrate both the progress and the remaining scale-up gaps, including semi-synthetic artemisinin, recombinant insulin, lactic acid, succinic acid, QS-21, and polyhydroxyalkanoates. The central argument is that the next phase of PF will depend less on isolated improvements in strain performance than on coordinated integration of strain design, intensified operation, real-time process understanding, and rigorous economic and environmental assessment. This integration is essential for translating laboratory performance into reproducible, scalable, and commercially credible biomanufacturing. KEY POINTS: PF requires integration of cell-factory engineering with scalable bioprocessing rather than optimisation of any single layer. DBTL and multi-omics improve strain performance, but laboratory titres do not guarantee industrial scalability. Bioprocess intensification and real-time monitoring are required to convert strain performance into robust production. PAT, soft sensors, and AI strengthen process control when supported by reliable online data and qualified models. TEA and LCA should be integrated early to filter commercial and environmental feasibility before scale-up.

works.title: Nuclear Functional Divergence and Genetic Basis of Cap Colour Variation Revealed by T2T Genomes of Two Compatible Monokaryons in Pholiota adiposa
works.abstract: Basidiomycete fungi maintain a dikaryotic state throughout their life cycle, in which two genetically distinct haploid nuclei coexist within the same cytoplasm. However, the extent and functional significance of inter-nuclear genomic divergence remain poorly understood. Here, we present the first telomere-to-telomere assemblies of two compatible monokaryons (D1 and D11) from a wild isolate of Pholiota adiposa, achieving 13 complete chromosomes with zero gaps and Benchmarking Universal Single-Copy Orthologs completeness of 98.6% and 98.3%, substantially outperforming the previous fragmented assembly. The two nuclei exhibit only 75% collinear genes, with 570 (D1) and 668 (D11) strain-specific genes. D1-specific genes are enriched in energy metabolism, consistent with faster mycelial growth, while D11-specific genes are enriched in genetic information processing and mitogen-activated protein kinase signalling, revealing functional complementarity between the two haploid nuclei. Resequencing of 18 wild accessions identified two candidate regions associated with red pileus colour on chromosomes 6 and 12, the former as a major-effect locus and the latter harbouring multiple pigment-associated genes. Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes enrichment implicated phenylalanine metabolism, tyrosine metabolism, and terpenoid biosynthesis in colour formation, suggesting coordinated regulation across metabolic networks. This framework facilitates dissection of nuclear functional divergence and provides candidate targets for understanding fungal phenotypic variation.

works.title: Corrigendum to “HIV-Gag VLP-based vaccine purification at manufacturing scale: Combination of counterflow centrifugation and nuclease treatment as a key to DNA depletion” [New Biotechnol. 93 (2026) 264–279/ISSN 1871–6784]
Improving Whole‐Cell Taxifolin Production Performance Through Growth‐coupled Directed Laboratory Evolution of Flavanone 3‐hydroxylase in Escherichia coli
works.abstract: ABSTRACT The unique hydroxylation pattern confers dihydroflavonols with multiple beneficial functions to human health. The bioproduction of dihydroflavonols is strictly driven by flavanone 3‐hydroxylase (F3H. This study focused on producing taxifolin, a typical high‐value dihydroflavonol. We established taxifolin synthesis route by substituting the plant‐derived flavonoid 3’‐hydroxylase (F3’H) with prokaryote‐derived two‐component 4HPA3H system (HpaB and HpaC). Kinetics of the production indicated that F3H is the rate‐limiting node. A directed library evolution (DLE) method was proposed to debottleneck this route. The tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle was rebuilt in Escherichia coli to couple DLE with cell growth. Very high transformation efficiency was achieved after medium optimization, thus facilitating the mutant library building. A library, theoretically containing 42360 mutants, was built and underwent a 4‐day DLE. Among the randomly picked out mutants, SlF3H v01 showed significantly accelerated catalytic rate. The whole‐cell containing SlF3H v01 produced 301.28% more taxifolin (93.82 mg/L) at 22 h and 29.73% more taxifolin (119.87 mg/L) at 46 h than that containing the wild type. This study built an E. coli chassis and developed an easy‐to‐manipulate DLE method to improve the taxifolin production. It can also be expanded to improve the performance of whole‐cell catalyst or microbial cell factory containing other α‐ketoglutarate‐dependent dioxygenase.

works.title: Correction to “Expanding Transposase Technology to Regulatory Noncoding RNAs for Stable Expression in CHO Cells”
works.abstract: S. Lochmueller, L. Weiss, and K. Otte, “Expanding Transposase Technology to Regulatory Noncoding RNAs for Stable Expression in CHO Cells,” Biotechnology Journal 21, no. 8 (2026): e70299, https://doi.org/10.1002/biot.70299. FIGURE 3: Effects of stable miRNA integration on CHO bioprocess parameters. (A) Viable cell density and (B) viability over a 5 day batch cultivation of CHO-monoclonal antibody (mAb)-producing cell pools stably expressing miR-3096b-5p via random and transposase-based integration. (C) Total antibody titers relative to mock and (D) specific productivity (Qp) after batch cultivation, assayed via analytical protein A chromatography. Significance was tested by ordinary one-way ANOVA (ns: p > 0.05) n = 3 technical triplicates, mean ± standard deviation. We apologize for this error.

works.title: Comparison of Wildtype and Recombinant Adeno‐Associated Virus (AAV) Production Reveals Distinct Productivity and Content Ratio Profiles
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Recombinant adeno‐associated virus is a leading viral vector for gene therapy. However, recombinant adeno‐associated virus production systems have low titer and content ratio (ratio of genome‐containing to total adeno‐associated virus capsids), making it difficult to generate the large number of vector genomes required for clinical or commercial use. In contrast, wildtype adeno‐associated virus achieves over ten‐fold higher titer compared to recombinant adeno‐associated virus and a content ratio of over 95% full. Despite the higher productivity of wildtype adeno‐associated virus, the mechanisms behind its productivity remain poorly understood. In this study, we developed and characterized a novel wildtype adeno‐associated virus production platform in suspension human embryonic kidney cells across varying multiplicities of infection of adeno‐associated virus to adenovirus. The impact of cellular viral genome delivery mechanisms and the interplay between adeno‐associated virus and its adenoviral helper were investigated by comparing infection‐based systems with transfection‐based and infection–transfection hybrid systems. Wildtype and hybrid infection systems had remarkably different host cell growth profiles and viral gene expression patterns, and achieved over a log‐fold higher titers and 45% higher content ratios, reaching 8.1 × 10 12 vector genomes/mL culture and 72.2% full, compared to recombinant transfection systems (1.63 × 10 11 vector genomes/mL and 26.9% full).

works.title: Fibroproliferative Remodeling of Immune‐Vascular Co‐Culture Spheroid Models in Response to Atherogenic Stimulation
works.abstract: Cell-based models are highly valuable platforms for preclinical studies of atherosclerosis, offering controllable environments to investigate disease mechanisms. Three-dimensional (3D) spheroids, a class of cell-based models, enable the study of atherosclerotic disease phenomena under physiologically relevant yet controlled conditions. In this study, we examined the lipid-induced changes in a co-culture spheroid model comprising THP-1-derived macrophages and primary human coronary artery smooth muscle cells (HCASMCs) following treatment with 20 or 40 µg/mL oxidized LDL (ox-LDL), a known atherogenic agent. Over a 10-day period, we assessed changes in spheroid morphology (size and compactness), cell viability, metabolic activity, intracellular composition, gene expression, pro-inflammatory cytokine release and extracellular matrix deposition, relative to the untreated control. Lipid exposure increased the abundance of macrophages in ox-LDL-treated spheroids (LS20-3 h: 35.5 ± 21.9%; LS40-3 h: 38.3 ± 8.7%) compared with controls (21.8 ± 0.7%) as early as day 3. Upregulation of fibronectin (LS20-3 h: ~1.8-fold; LS40-3 h: ~2.1-fold), CD36 (~1.8-fold), and ABCA-1 (~1.9-fold) was also observed. Moreover, spheroids exposed to 40 µg/mL ox-LDL exhibited reduced viability and compactness compared with those treated with 20 µg/mL by day 10. While lipid-treated spheroids showed non-statistically significantly higher levels of pro-inflammatory IL-1β cytokine expression at day 0 which declined (> 85% decrease) by day 3, all spheroid groups showed comparable global fibronectin ECM secretion indices. Collectively, these findings reveal lipid-induced proliferative changes to spheroid composition & functionality and show their potential as biomimetic models for the study of atherosclerotic disease phenomena.

works.title: Cac3319 Inactivation Sustains Solventogenesis Through Proteomic and Phosphoregulatory Remodeling in Clostridium acetobutylicum
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Clostridium acetobutylicum is a promising biofuel producer for acetone‐butanol‐ethanol (ABE) fermentation, yet sustained butanol production is constrained by the short duration of solventogenic activity. Although the orphan histidine kinase Cac3319 has been implicated in Spo0A phosphorylation, sporulation, and solvent production, metabolic and phosphorylation changes following cac3319 inactivation have not been systematically characterized. Here, we integrated fermentation kinetics, comparative proteomics, and Ti 4+ ‐IMAC phosphoproteomics to investigate the effects of cac3319 inactivation in C. acetobutylicum ATCC 55025. The cac3319 knockout prolonged late‐stage metabolic activity without impairing early growth, enabling continued glucose utilization and solvent accumulation after entry into solventogenesis. Final butanol and total ABE titers increased from 13.0 to 17.5 g L −1 and from 18.5 to 28.5 g L −1 , respectively. Proteomic analysis revealed increased protein abundance spanning central carbon metabolism, acid reassimilation, energy metabolism, and protein protection. Phosphoproteomic analysis further revealed phase‐dependent remodeling of detectable phosphorylation events, indicating that post‐translational regulation was reshaped during the acidogenic‐to‐solventogenic transition. These coordinated changes supported a metabolically active and stress‐tolerant state conducive to sustained solventogenesis. Collectively, these findings provide new insights into histidine kinase‐mediated regulation of clostridial solventogenesis and highlight cac3319 inactivation as a promising strategy for sustaining late‐stage metabolic activity and improving butanol production in ABE fermentation.

works.title: Agentic Artificial Intelligence‐Driven Neutrosophic Multi‐Objective Optimization of Oxygen Transfer Systems in Smart Bioreactors
works.abstract: Oxygen transfer control in industrial bioreactors becomes more complex when cell metabolic changes, nonlinear process dynamics, energy constraints, and biological and operational uncertainties simultaneously affect control decisions. This study presents an innovative framework for intelligent oxygenation management that integrates a synchronized digital twin, agent-based artificial intelligence, fuzzy-notrosophic modeling, and multi-objective decision-making in a closed, uncertainty-aware loop. The proposed framework enables predictive and safe decision-making under variable conditions by continuously monitoring and reconstructing the process state, predicting short-term behavior, generating and screening control options, and virtually evaluating them before implementation. Evaluation under normal operating conditions and biological and process disturbances showed that the complete framework achieved 98.04% dissolved oxygen stability and reduced the recovery time after oxygen demand shock to 7.26 min. The findings show that the main value of this architecture lies not in the single maximization of oxygen transfer, but in creating an adaptive balance between oxygen delivery, energy consumption, shear stress, biological stability, and operational risk. This framework provides an extensible platform for moving toward autonomous, resilient, and sustainable bioreactors.

works.title: Yeast Surface Display of Artificial Multienzyme Complexes for Enhanced Production of Rebaudioside M
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Rebaudioside M (Reb M) is an ideal low‐calorie natural sweetener with excellent sensory properties and well‐established safety profile. Industrial production of Reb M is limited by low natural abundance and the bottlenecks of existing biomanufacturing strategies, including low productivity, intermediate accumulation and high enzyme costs. Here, a novel biosynthetic platform based on yeast surface display of artificial multienzyme complexes was established for efficient Reb M production. The artificial protein scaffold containing multiple orthogonal cohesin modules was displayed on the surface of Pichia pastoris via the AGA1 anchoring motif. Through orthogonal cohesin‐dockerin interactions, Reb M biosynthetic pathway enzymes (PgUGT Mut , AtSUS1 and UGT76G1 Mut ) with the corresponding dockerin modules were assembled on the artificial protein scaffold to form multienzyme complexes. The catalytic activity of crude glycosyltransferases was improved by isozyme screening and expression optimization with molecular chaperones. This surface‐displayed system demonstrated multiple advantages. First, the multienzyme complex assembled on the yeast surface showed higher catalytic efficiency than free enzymes. Additionally, fructose was consumed by P. pastoris to drive the reaction toward Reb M biosynthesis. Furthermore, the whole‐cell catalyst showed promising reusability. Ultimately, this platform enabled the production of 36.88 g/L Reb M with a yield of 91.9% from rebaudioside A (Reb A) in a 10 mL reaction system. This work provided a feasible strategy to address the key bottlenecks in Reb M biomanufacturing and offered a reference for producing other high‐value natural products via multi‐enzyme cascade catalysis.

works.title: Kinetics Based on the Rapid‑Equilibrium Approach for the Reduction of an Achiral Ketone to a Chiral Alcohol by a Single Carbonyl Reductase With NAD(P)H Regeneration Using Isopropyl Alcohol as the Hydrogen Donor
works.abstract: The kinetics of a single-enzyme, substrate-coupled system in batch operation for the asymmetric production of chiral alcohols from achiral ketones through NAD(P)H regeneration-using isopropyl alcohol (IPA) as a hydrogen donor-were investigated. Assuming the effective removal of acetone, two novel mathematical equations were derived by applying the rapid equilibrium approach to four enzyme-substrate complexes: one for the chiral alcohol formation rate, and another modeling its concentration over time under the assumption of a constant IPA concentration. The formation rate equation for batch operation was transformed into a dimensionless form to elucidate how constituent variables and parameters affect the reaction rate. The derived rate equations, which are two-parameter mathematical models, are substantially simpler than those in previously reported studies. The derived product formation rate decreases monotonically and remarkably with reaction time, agreeing with experimental results reported across the literature. The proposed time-course equation was validated against experimental data from two published studies. The fit of the derived equations to the experimental data was satisfactory within acceptable deviations, provided the core assumptions were satisfied.

works.title: Batch‐to‐Batch Optimization of pH Shifts in CHO Bioreactor Operations
works.abstract: Culture pH is an important operating parameter in CHO cell cultures producing mAb since it directly affects growth and specific productivity. Mathematical models can be used to optimize the magnitude and timing of pH shifts provided that they are robust to model errors. To address model errors, we implement, for the first time experimentally, a robust batch-to-batch optimization procedure that iteratively adjusts the model by updating model parameters and by matching predicted to measured gradients of the objective function and constraints at each iteration. A dynamic metabolic flux model with pH-dependent kinetic constraints was used for optimization. The approach was applied experimentally using a system of micro-bioreactors, leading to an improvement of the titer up to 18% compared to the nominal experimental conditions. The necessity of gradient matching to compensate for model errors was clearly demonstrated by comparing experiments conducted with and without gradient matching. The mathematical model also allowed the identification of metabolic mechanisms that contribute to the observed improvements in productivity.

works.title: Metabolic Remodelingof the NOG Pathway and Glyoxylate Cycle for High‐Yield L‐Homoserine Biosynthesis
works.abstract: L‑homoserine is a valuable C4 amino acid with broad applications in agriculture, pharmaceuticals, and daily chemicals. However, existing high‑yielding strains have mainly been evaluated at laboratory scale, and their scale‑up feasibility has not yet been sufficiently verified, leaving industrial production without a direct engineering basis. In this study, a non-auxotrophic, scalable L‑homoserine high‑producer was constructed by targeting carbon loss, rewiring the metabolic network, and maintaining cofactor balance. Specifically, the threonine branch was dynamically attenuated to reduce product degradation, while the non‑oxidative glycolysis (NOG) pathway was introduced and coupled with the glyoxylate shunt to conserve carbon and redirect flux toward the aspartate pathway, thereby increasing precursor availability. The main biosynthetic pathway and cofactor regeneration were further strengthened to accelerate L‑homoserine synthesis. Ultimately, strain HS25 achieved a titer of 126.5 g/L L‑homoserine,a yield of 0.58 g/g glucose, and a productivity of 1.77 g/L/hin 50 L fermentation. These metabolic engineering strategies are scalable and may serve as a generalizable framework for the industrial production of other aspartate‑derived amino acids and their derivatives.

works.title: 10‐Fold Improvement in Depth Filter Capacity During Integrated Dynamic Bioprocessing (IDB) Purification Through Depth Filter Cycling and Precipitate Control Strategy
works.abstract: ABSTRACT During bsAb1 purification, precipitate was formed during neutralization of the affinity capture product. This precipitate was removed before loading onto the first polishing column in the Integrated Dynamic Bioprocessing (IDB) platform. The precipitate had a dynamic particle size distribution that caused complex scaling without proper characterization. Herein, the study established a protocol for characterizing downstream precipitate formation and operating a depth filter (Emphaze AEX) like a chromatography column to support continuous purification of bsAb1. The depth filter is “underloaded” with precipitated material, followed by a chase step and the application of sanitization buffers. The sanitization buffers solubilized precipitate bound to the depth filter and controlled bioburden, drastically increasing the filter capacity and helped ensure a closed system. At the bench, the depth filter was cycled 40 times for a total capacity of 10,500 L/m 2 . This capacity is an order of magnitude greater than when the depth filter is loaded to max capacity without any cycling or sanitization. The resulting cycling capacity eases depth filter scale‐up and IDB implementation at the clinical and commercial scale.

works.title: From cherry-pit biomass to N,S-doped carbon quantum dots: Linking synthesis conditions to photophysical properties and chromium detection
works.abstract: Converting agricultural waste into functional carbon quantum dots offers a sustainable approach to developing fluorescent nanomaterials for environmental monitoring. However, achieving desirable photophysical properties and sensing performance requires careful control of synthesis conditions and precursor composition. Herein, nitrogen- and sulfur-doped carbon quantum dots (N,S-CQDs) were synthesized in a one-pot microwave-assisted hydrothermal treatment from cherry-pit biomass using L-cysteine as a heteroatom source and evaluated in terms of their photophysical characteristics and sensitivity to chromium species. The N,S-CQDs demonstrated nanoscale dimensions and exhibited favorable photoluminescence properties, where the quantum yield increased from 19% to 30.5% with increasing L-cysteine content. The fluorescence response exhibited a linear pattern across the pH range of 5 to 9, with the highest emission recorded at pH 9. This observation establishes a foundation for subsequent chromium sensing. The N,S-CQDs demonstrated a concentration-dependent response toward Cr(VI), with a detection limit of 1.25 μM over 0–80 μM, whereas Cr(III) produced no appreciable response. Following oxidative conversion of Cr(III) to Cr(VI) using H₂O₂, indirect Cr(III) determination was achieved with a detection limit of 1.8 μM over 0–100 μM. The probe showed good tolerance toward representative interfering species and maintained its fluorescence response under storage, UV irradiation, varied ionic strengths, and various solvent conditions. Spectral overlap suggested a substantial contribution of the inner filter effect to the fluorescence quenching, while FT-IR, XPS, and zeta-potential analyses after Cr(VI) sensing proposed additional surface interactions and complexation between Cr(VI) and the CQD functional groups.

works.title: Chemical modification of immobilized eversa enhances its performance in the hydrolysis of castor oil under optimal conditions
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Eversa® Transform 2.0 (ETL) was immobilized onto hydrophobic octadecyl-coated methacrylate beads via interfacial activation (ETL@C18). Subsequently, ETL@C18 was treated with glutaraldehyde (ETL@C18-Glu) or ethylenediamine (ETL@C18-EDA). The biocatalysts were used in the hydrolysis of castor oil. Under standard conditions, ETL@C18 showed the best performance (42.8% of hydrolysis and a productivity of 598.2 mmol/(h·g of protein) in 24 h). Then, the reaction catalyzed by each biocatalyst was optimized using the Taguchi method for all biocatalysts varying reactor temperature, substrate ratio, biocatalyst content and stirring level. Optimal conditions differed for each biocatalyst. ETL@C18-Glu was the most efficient biocatalyst under its optimal conditions (50 °C, 1:1 oil/water, 5 wt.% of biocatalyst and 200 rpm), reaching 90% of hydrolysis. Under its respective optimized conditions, ETL@C18 exhibited a similar hydrolysis yield, but requiring higher biocatalyst content (9 wt.%) and, thus, exhibited lower productivity than ETL@C18-Glu (138.45 vs. 250.58 mmol/h·g protein). Nevertheless, ETL@C18-EDA exhibited the highest operational stability, retaining 87% of its initial hydrolytic activity after 5 reaction cycles (versus 74% and 71.5% for ETL@C18 and ETL@C18-Glu, respectively). Thus, the ranking of the biocatalysts under standard conditions was not maintained after optimization, because the chemical modifications changed the response of the enzyme to the reaction conditions.

works.title: Optimization of integrated enzymatic-thermal hydrolysis of pear pomace to produce sugar-rich hydrolysates with sweetening potential
Cysteine-mediated redox strategy for enhancing desired heterodimer formation in KiH-based antibody purification
works.abstract: Although Knobs-into-Holes (KiH) technology effectively promotes heterodimer formation in bispecific antibodies, product-related impurities, including half-antibody species, are frequently generated during manufacturing. Owing to their similar physicochemical properties, these impurities are often difficult to separate from the target antibody using conventional chromatographic methods. Here, we present a cysteine-mediated redox strategy that improves product quality by reassembling these product-related impurities into desired heterodimers, rather than removing them. We implemented two process strategies: a cysteine-supplemented wash step during Protein A affinity chromatography (PA) and a cysteine-mediated batch reaction prior to polishing chromatography. Design of experiments (DoE) identified cysteine concentration as the critical process parameter controlling heterodimer reassembly ( p < 0.05) across both strategies. The cysteine-integrated process consistently improved reversed-phase high-performance liquid chromatography (RP-HPLC) purity while preserving the structural integrity of the target antibody. Peptide mapping and disulfide bond analysis revealed that the cysteine-integrated process promotes inter-chain disulfide bond rearrangement, leading to correct heterodimer assembly, thereby reducing mispaired species and increasing the abundance of correctly assembled heterodimers compared with the conventional process. Remarkably, the cysteine-integrated process achieved approximately a 1.9-fold higher cumulative yield than the conventional approach at an equivalent RP-HPLC purity (>90%). The process was successfully scaled up to a 200 L pilot scale without compromising process performance, demonstrating its scalability and robustness. Collectively, these findings establish the cysteine-mediated redox strategy as a practical, scalable, and manufacturing-compatible approach for improving both product quality and process efficiency in the production of heterodimeric bispecific antibodies.

works.title: Maoyu Extract Suppresses Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Progression via PI3K/AKT Signaling Blockade: An Integrated Network Pharmacology and Experimental Validation Study
Harnessing engineered laccase and functional carrier materials for efficient dye degradation: From mechanism to application
works.abstract: Laccases are copper-containing oxidases that have been widely investigated for the decolorization and degradation of synthetic dyes, including azo, anthraquinone, triphenylmethane, indigo and thiazine dyes. However, their application in dye-containing wastewater remains constrained by enzyme instability under complex effluent conditions, limited oxidation of some recalcitrant or high-redox-potential dyes, mediator dependence, and poor recovery and reuse of free laccase. This review discusses recent progress in laccase-catalyzed dye degradation from a mechanism-to-engineering perspective, linking dye-structure-dependent degradation pathways with laccase discovery, recombinant expression, protein engineering and immobilization strategies. Particular attention is given to comparative evidence across dye classes, fungal and bacterial laccases, engineered variants generated through rational design, directed evolution and semi-rational mutagenesis, and immobilized laccase systems based on nanomaterials, biopolymers, magnetic carriers and porous supports. In addition, the review distinguishes laboratory model dye systems from simulated and real wastewater applications, highlighting the need for more cautious interpretation of decolorization efficiency, degradation evidence and process feasibility. Finally, we outline future prospects for laccase applications in dye degradation, including the mining of novel laccases from extreme environments, artificial intelligence-assisted laccase design, and developing new nano-scale carrier materials, which will be essential for enhancing laccase performance and broadening its application scope.

works.title: Exploring endophytic actinomycetes from Shiraia fruiting bodies to enhance fungal hypocrellin A biosynthesis
works.abstract: The medicinal fruiting bodies of Shiraia harbor diverse microbial communities that are increasingly recognized as important regulators of fungal secondary metabolism. While endophytic bacteria and fungi associated with Shiraia have recently attracted considerable attention, the diversity and functional roles of endophytic actinomycetes remain largely unexplored. Here, we combined culture-dependent isolation with high-throughput 16 S rRNA amplicon sequencing to investigate the endophytic actinomycete community associated with Shiraia fruiting bodies. A total of 28 actinomycete isolates representing four genera were recovered, with Streptomyces being the predominant culturable genus. Functional screening identified the native endophyte S. pseudogriseolus A6 as the most effective elicitor of fungal hypocrellin A (HA) biosynthesis. Genome analysis revealed abundant carbohydrate-active enzymes and 27 secondary metabolite biosynthetic gene clusters, indicating a strong genetic potential for fungal colonization and metabolite-mediated communication. Co-cultivation with live strain A6 markedly enhanced both intracellular and extracellular HA accumulation without significantly affecting fungal biomass. Under the optimized co-cultivation conditions, total HA production reached 296.0 mg/L, representing a threefold increase over the monoculture control. Furthermore, A6 coordinately upregulated the expression of HA biosynthetic genes and metabolite transport genes. This study provides the first characterization of endophytic actinomycetes associated with Shiraia fruiting bodies and identifies actinomycete elicitors capable of stimulating fungal HA biosynthesis. These findings expand current knowledge of the Shiraia microbiome and highlight endophytic actinomycetes as promising microbial resources for enhancing fungal perylenequinone production.

works.title: What drives the cost of biowaste-to-lipase production? Linking titre, rate and yield to techno-economic performance in batch-to-continuous Pichia pastoris fermentation
works.abstract: Fruit and vegetable (FV) waste represents an underutilized organic stream in Europe, yet its soluble sugar fraction remains poorly exploited as a bioprocess feedstock. Recombinant enzyme production from biowaste is often bottlenecked by heterogeneous substrate composition, low fermentable sugar titres, and uncertain process economics. This study evaluates the techno-economic feasibility of recombinant Candida rugosa lipase type 1 (CRL1) production in Pichia pastoris (Komagataella phaffii) under the constitutive glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase promoter pGAP across three carbon sources: commercial glucose (Scenario A), mechanically pressed fruit and vegetable juice (Scenario B), and an enzymatically hydrolysed, nanofiltered fruit and vegetablesugar stream (Scenario C). Bench-scale fermentation kinetics were integrated into 24 SuperPro Designer models across four scales (1 to 5000 L nominal vessel capacity; 0.75 to 3750 L working volume) under batch and continuous chemostat ( $$\:D=0.05 {\text{h}}^{-1}$$ ) modes. Interpreted through the Titre, Rate, and Yield (TRY) framework, continuous operation on glucose increased volumetric CRL1 productivity 12.6-fold over batch (0.084 vs. 0.06 U L−1 h−1. Conversely, continuous operation on the hydrolysed stream did not improve productivity over batch, indicating potential kinetic inhibition from enzymatic pretreatment products or suboptimal dilution rate. At the 5000 L vessel scale under continuous mode, unit production costs were $1186, $36,049, and $3416 $$\:{\text{kg}}^{-1}$$ for Scenarios A, B, and C, respectively, all exceeding the commodity lipase benchmark ($25 $$\:{\text{kg}}^{-1}$$ ). Facility-dependent costs dominated Scenarios A and B (73% and 78% of OPEX), whereas enzyme reagents dominated Scenario C (75%). Sensitivity analysis confirmed that secreted protein titre and downstream recovery efficiency are the primary economic drivers, demonstrating that feedstock acquisition cost is not the binding constraint. Early-stage TEA driven by bench-scale kinetic parameterization provides essential screening prior to pilot-scale investment in biowaste-to-enzyme biorefineries.

A mosaic T7 phage platform enables simultaneous display of two independent peptides on the same phage particle. The modular design integrates receptor targeting, protein capture, and tissue-directed in vivo phage display, establishing a versatile methodology for multifunctional phage engineering, receptor identification, and next-generation combinatorial library design.

works.title: Improving methanol tolerance and utilization of Saccharomyces cerevisiae via SCRaMbLE and systematic metabolic engineering
Biosynthesis of β-farnesene, a renewable biofuel precursor, from lignin-removed biomass residues using engineered Saccharomyces cerevisiae
Repeated xylitol production by immobilized Gluconobacter oxydans using diatom frustule–alginate composite carriers
works.abstract: Abstract Xylitol, a common sugar substitute in food and pharmaceuticals, can be produced microbially using glucose as the primary substrate. Our earlier study established an efficient one-step biotransformation system in Gluconobacter oxydans that converts D-arabitol to xylitol. To improve the reusability of resting cells, recombinant G. oxydans was immobilized in a composite matrix of Cyclotella meneghiniana frustules and solium alginate. The combined approach not only enhanced the mechanical strength and stability of the beads but also facilitated mass and oxygen transfer. Compared with frustules adsorption and alginate encapsulation alone, the combined immobilized cells exhibited increases in catalytic activity of 32.8% and 17.3%, respectively. An in-situ immobilization protocol, adding 2.0 g/L frustules to the fermentation medium with a 22 h culture time, further improved immobilized cell activity by 17.3%.
