The analysis of the biotransformation fractions by gas chromatography coupled with mass spectrometry (GC-MS), based on the interpretation of fragmentation patterns obtained by electron ionization (EI), enabled the tentative proposal of the structures of seven new triterpenoid derivatives. The spectral data further indicate that these compounds mainly belong to the ∆12-oleanane and ∆12-ursene structural families. The in vitro cytotoxic activity evaluation of all fractions revealed significantly higher activity of the triterpenoid fractions compared to the non-triterpenoid fractions at a concentration of 50 µg/mL. F9 showed significant inhibitory activity against the LS174T cell line (IC50 = 30.5 µg/mL), while F3 showed significant inhibitory activity against the HCT116 cell line (IC50 = 26.4 µg/mL). This study highlights the potential of bioconversion as an eco-friendly strategy for the valorization of valuable natural products, thereby opening the way to new bioactive molecules.

works.title: Scalable production of highly enriched chitobiose shows promise in agriculture, promoting plant growth and bolstering immunity
works.abstract: Abstract Chitobiose is a high-value, chitin-derived disaccharide with promising potential for agricultural application. Unfortunately, current production methods rely on hazardous chemical and costly enzymatic processing and the resulting high cost prohibits its commercial application. In this work, we report a simple, scalable fermentation platform, based on a Streptomyces venezuelae ΔdasBC transporter mutant that converts raw chitin directly into chitobiose. By tuning production parameters to maximize titer, the process yielded an estimated ~ 450 mg/L chitobiose without chitin pretreatment or enzymatic steps. Liquid chromatography/mass spectrometry showed the product to be highly enriched for chitobiose with the absence of detectable longer N-acetylglucosamine oligomers. To explore the potential agricultural application, we tested the crude spent medium as a biostimulant. As a soil additive, it increased Arabidopsis thaliana rosette size by up to 22% and induced beneficial changes to root development, while foliar pretreatment decreased Botrytis cinerea infection symptoms and increased the immunity-related responses to fungal elicitors. Notably, this immune-priming activity surpassed that of a commercially available chitin oligomer mix at an equivalent mass concentration, highlighting its potency. Together, this work establishes a cost-effective microbial platform for the production of highly enriched chitobiose and demonstrates its utility as a bioproduct that promotes plant growth and defense. The approach enables sustainable valorization of chitin waste streams into a defined, bioactive molecule for agriculture applications.

works.title: How the seminal work of a giant shaped the research of the next generation
Recombinant sucrose isomerases in Pichia pastoris for the production of isomaltulose as an alternative sweetener
Microbial cell factories for gamma-linolenic acid biosynthesis: metabolic engineering, downstream processing, and future perspectives
works.abstract: Gamma-linolenic acid (GLA) is a vital anti-inflammatory polyunsaturated fatty acid, yet its traditional supply from plant seeds such as evening primrose and borage is constrained by low yields and climatic instability. Consequently, microbial cell factories present a sustainable and season-independent alternative for scalable GLA production. This review critically synthesizes recent biotechnological advancements in utilizing oleaginous microorganisms as production platforms. It systematically elucidates the microbial lipid biosynthesis pathways and evaluates strategies to enhance GLA accumulation, with particular emphasis on rational metabolic engineering. Furthermore, emerging technologies for microbial lipid production, alongside the latest progress in industrial-scale applications, are thoroughly examined. Finally, comprehensive insights are provided to guide the optimization of the entire value chain, ranging from upstream strain engineering to downstream processing.

works.title: Orchestrating polyketide synthase-derived aldehyde metabolism for Streptomyces biomanufacturing
works.abstract: Advances in metabolic engineering have enabled the integration of diverse non-native reactions into microbial hosts, providing sustainable alternatives to petrochemical manufacturing. We previously developed a modular polyketide synthase (PKS)-based platform in Streptomyces albus for producing 17 diols, amino alcohols, and hydroxy acids. In this platform, terminal thioester reductases (TRs) release aldehyde intermediates that are subsequently converted by post-PKS enzymes to control product chemistry. Here we found that PKS-TR strains accumulated hundreds of genome-wide single-nucleotide variants, including missense mutations on conserved PKS and TR residues leading to impaired enzyme activity. Based on the hypothesis of aldehyde toxicity, we coupled TR catalysis with downstream alcohol dehydrogenases (ADHs) through gene co-integration or PKS-TR-ADH fusion to limit aldehyde accumulation. These strategies reduced genomic variability and increased diol production, reaching a total diol titer of 14.2 g/L in bioreactors, including 10.8 g/L 1,3-butanediol. Extending this approach, engineered strains incorporating PKS-TR co-integration with transaminases or the padA aldehyde dehydrogenase achieved 79% higher total amino alcohol titers and 145% higher 2-methyl-3-hydroxyhexanoic acid titer than previous reports, while eliminating diol byproducts from the optimized hydroxy acid pathway. These results establish TR-mediated aldehyde release as a programmable branch point and orchestrated downstream catalysis as a general strategy for improving the stability, productivity, and selectivity of PKS-based Streptomyces biomanufacturing.

works.title: Bottom-up design of native bacterial consortia improves Chlorella sorokiniana growth performance and vitamin B12 content from laboratory to pilot scale
works.abstract: Abstract Interactions between microalgae and associated bacteria can enhance growth performance and biomass quality, yet their evaluation beyond laboratory scale remains limited. Here, 124 bacterial strains were isolated from industrial autotrophic Chlorella sorokiniana cultures and rationally assembled into a three-member consortium (MC-3) comprising Comamonas koreensis , Pseudomonas fluorescens , and Stenotrophomonas rhizophila through structured pairwise and multi-strain screening. At laboratory scale, MC-3 doubled the specific growth rate and enriched methylcobalamin (MeCbl) content by up to 19-fold relative to axenic controls. Validation in 100-L flat-panel photobioreactors (FP-PBR) and 2.5 m³ tubular photobioreactors (T-PBR) confirmed that MC-3 increased final cell concentration, by 30% in the FP-PBRs and 62% in the T-PBRs, and enriched MeCbl by 56% and 59%, respectively, while maintaining overall biochemical stability. Phytohormone profiling in the T-PBRs revealed lower 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylic acid levels and higher gibberellin and auxin concentrations in MC-3 cultures, indicating a system-level correlation between consortium inoculation and growth-promoting hormonal shifts. Finally, consortium persistence across production systems was confirmed by 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing. These results demonstrate that ecologically compatible bacterial consortia can be rationally designed from industrial microbiomes and deployed as scalable tools to improve both productivity and nutritional value of C. sorokiniana under real production conditions.

works.title: Eco-friendly biosynthesis of silver nanoparticles by saprophytic Fusarium solani as a sustainable therapeutic approach for the management of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus wound infections
works.abstract: The rising prevalence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has prompted the exploration of novel, naturally sourced therapeutic alternatives. Here, the saprophytic fungus Fusarium solani was used to biosynthesize silver nanoparticles (AgNPs), which were characterized by UV-visible spectroscopy, transmission electron microscopy (TEM), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR). The AgNPs showed a surface plasmon resonance peak at ~ 410 nm, a zeta potential of - 42.7 mV, an average TEM diameter of 19.58 nm, and a hydrodynamic (DLS) diameter of 121.4 nm with a polydispersity index of 0.302. Against clinical methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) isolates, the AgNPs exhibited minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) and minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) values of 0.1875-0.375 mM, with confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) showing a reduction in bacterial viability from 92.3% to 28.0% and TEM revealing marked ultrastructural membrane damage following treatment. In a murine MRSA wound infection model, AgNPs treatment increased wound healing from 12.33% to 95.33% and reduced bacterial load from 9.90 to 1.10 log CFU/g tissue relative to the untreated infected control, alongside significant downregulation of TNF-α, IL-6, and COX-2 expression and improved histopathological indices of tissue repair (all p < 0.05). These findings indicate that fungal-derived AgNPs possess potent antibacterial and wound-healing properties against MRSA, supporting their potential as a sustainable therapeutic candidate, although further mechanistic and translational studies are needed.

works.title: Multi-parameter optimization of recombinant protein secretion in Bacillus subtilis: a review
works.abstract: Bacillus subtilis is widely recognized as one of the most robust and versatile hosts for recombinant protein production. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the protein secretion pathway in B. subtilis, detailing its mechanistic basis and key limiting steps. We discuss the structural features of signal peptides (SPs) that govern efficient translocation and highlight recent advances in de novo promoter and signal peptide engineering. A particular focus is placed on the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) to predict and design optimal genetic elements. Drawing on findings from combinatorial and multi-parameter studies, we propose that future engineering strategies should move beyond maximizing individual parameters. Instead, achieving a dynamic balance across transcriptional, translational and secretion layers is essential to sustain high productivity while minimizing cellular secretion stress. This review offers a roadmap for systems-level engineering of B. subtilis as a next-generation protein production platform.

works.title: Occupational environments are associated with distinct oral and gut microbiome–metabolome profiles
works.abstract: The profound health impacts of distinct long-term work environments, such as indoor sedentary versus outdoor physical labor, remain poorly understood at the microbial and metabolic levels. To address this, we used an integrated metagenomic and metabolomic approach to systematically compare the oral and gut ecosystems of indoor sedentary workers (university teachers) and outdoor physical laborers (construction and transportation workers). Our analysis revealed stark, niche-specific differences. Outdoor laborers showed higher salivary microbial diversity, whereas indoor workers had higher gut microbial diversity coupled with a marked reduction in microbial resistance genes. Crucially, statistical mediation analysis of the ‘environment-microbiome-metabolite’ axis uncovered fundamentally different regulatory logics in the two niches. The oral ecosystem operated on a ‘push-and-pull’ model of mixed mediation; notably, the indoor sedentary lifestyle was positively associated with the key metabolic risk marker, uric acid, statistically mediated by a reduced abundance of purine-competing Prevotella species. In contrast, the gut ecosystem displayed a highly uniform ‘many-to-one’ architecture, where diverse microbial shifts converged to statistically mediate a reduction in a small set of metabolites, primarily a single exogenous steroid derivative. Furthermore, these multi-omics signatures were highly predictive, with salivary metabolome data distinguishing the two groups with up to 98.04% accuracy. This study suggests that multi-omics profiles may serve as a sensitive ‘biological archive’ of an individual’s work environment. These highly predictive signatures are promising candidates for biomarker development in health monitoring and forensic inference, and highlight potential microbe-metabolite targets for future intervention studies tailored to lifestyle-specific risks.

works.title: Taxonomic, biochemical, and genome-guided characterization of Halomonas elongata N1T reveals its potential as a sustainable microbial cell factory for human lectin-binding exopolysaccharide production
works.abstract: Microbial exopolysaccharides (EPSs) have attracted considerable attention as sustainable biopolymers for applications in the food, pharmaceutical, cosmetic and environmental sectors. Halophilic bacteria of the genus Halomonas are emerging as attractive industrial production hosts because their ability to grow under saline conditions reduces contamination risks and may enable cost-effective, low-sterility bioprocesses. However, relatively few EPS-producing Halomonas strains have been comprehensively characterized by integrating physiological, genomic and structural analyses. In this study, an EPS-producing halophilic bacterium, designated Halomonas elongata N1T, was isolated from the hypersaline Salt Lake of Yerevan, Armenia, and evaluated as a potential microbial cell factory for sustainable EPS production. Phylogenomic analyses confirmed its affiliation with H. elongata , showing 98.9% average nucleotide identity and 90.9% digital DNA–DNA hybridization with the type strain DSM 2581 T . Genome analysis identified multiple carbohydrate-active enzymes together with three major polysaccharide biosynthetic gene clusters containing canonical ABC transporter-dependent export proteins and numerous glycosyltransferases, providing a genetic basis for EPS biosynthesis. Cultivation under buffered saline conditions markedly enhanced polymer production, yielding up to 517 mg L −1 crude exoproduct, while inexpensive sugarcane molasses supported comparable production levels to sucrose, demonstrating the feasibility of using an agro-industrial by-product as a carbon source. Chemical characterization revealed a high-molecular-weight (approximately 250–500 kDa) heteropolysaccharide composed primarily of rhamnose, glucosamine, glucose and ribose, and preliminary NMR analysis confirmed its structural heterogeneity. In addition, the purified EPS exhibited a binding to the human C-type lectins Langerin and DC-SIGN, suggesting potential biological functionality beyond conventional industrial applications. The integration of physiological characterization, comparative genomics, EPS biosynthetic pathway analysis and polymer characterization demonstrates that H. elongata N1T is a promising candidate for sustainable EPS production. Its ability to efficiently synthesize EPS under saline conditions while utilizing an inexpensive renewable substrate highlights its potential as a microbial cell factory for future industrial bioprocesses. The unique genomic features and lectin-binding properties of the polymer further broaden its prospective applications in biotechnology and biomedicine.

works.title: Transcriptome-guided identification of YALI0_F02013g and YALI0_A19910g as candidate NADPH-dependent oxidoreductases associated with enhanced erythritol production in Yarrowia lipolytica
works.abstract: NADPH competition by non-erythrose-reductase oxidoreductases limits erythritol yields in Yarrowia lipolytica , yet the specific contributors remain poorly defined. This study characterised two candidate genes, YALI0_F02013g (putative pyridoxine 4-dehydrogenase) and YALI0_A19910g (putative glycerol 2-dehydrogenase), using time-resolved transcriptomics, molecular docking and metabolic modelling. RNA-seq analysis across 96 h of fermentation revealed distinct temporal profiles: YALI0_F02013g was progressively induced 3.4-fold (peak 5040 FPKM at 72 h), while YALI0_A19910g was repressed 920-fold by 96 h (Table 2). Expression trends were validated by qRT-PCR (Pearson r > 0.94; Table 3). YALI0_A19910g expression correlated strongly negatively with erythritol titre (Pearson r = − 0.858), whereas YALI0_F02013g showed a weak positive correlation. Molecular docking predicted high NADPH binding affinities for both enzymes (− 9.8 and − 8.6 kcal mol⁻ 1 , respectively; Fig. 2) and identified conserved catalytic triads. An integrated prioritisation model ranked YALI0_F02013g as the higher-priority target (5.6/10 vs 5.0/10; Table 7). In silico flux estimates suggest that repressing YALI0_F02013g could conserve approximately 67% of the competing NADPH demand, potentially increasing erythritol yield by ~14%; these projections require experimental validation (Table 8). These findings identify YALI0_F02013g as a candidate metabolic bottleneck in the strain background examined, offering a specific target for engineering improved cofactor efficiency in industrial Yarrowia lipolytica strains.

works.title: CO2 availability shapes acetate and ethanol production in Clostridium aceticum: a transcriptomics-guided study
works.abstract: Clostridium aceticum , a model acetogen utilizing the Wood–Ljungdahl pathway (WLP), offers a promising microbial platform for converting CO 2 -rich syngas into value-added biofuels. In this study, we systematically investigated the effects of varying CO 2 concentrations on fermentation kinetics and global transcriptional responses of C. aceticum . Acetate production increased steadily with higher CO 2 levels, reaching 12.3 g/L at 45% CO 2 , whereas ethanol accumulation peaked at 25% CO 2 , suggesting a metabolic trade-off between acid and alcohol formation. Elevated CO 2 enhanced biomass formation and product titer, but accelerated acidification, thereby constraining cell growth at very high concentrations. Comparative transcriptomics revealed 246 differentially expressed genes, with key CO 2 fixation genes ( acsA1 and fdhF ) and ethanol biosynthesis genes ( ald and adh ) upregulated, while ATP-dependent steps of the WLP, such as fhs , were repressed, reflecting intrinsic energy limitations. Notably, the upregulation of L-serine dehydratase and formate-acetyltransferase implicated serine metabolism as an alternative route to acetyl-CoA, providing formate and CO 2 to support the WLP. Guided by these insights, exogenous L-serine supplementation increased intracellular ATP by 1.95-fold, and enhanced acetate and ethanol titer by 23.3% and 12.5%, respectively. These findings highlight CO 2 availability as a central regulator of carbon flux and energy metabolism in C. aceticum and propose amino acid supplementation as a practical strategy to improve syngas fermentation efficiency.

works.title: Next-generation nano-biocatalysts: extremozyme-based nanoparticle system for cypermethrin bioremediation
works.abstract: Abstract Extremozymes, with their exceptional catalytic activity and stability under extreme environmental conditions, have great potential for pesticide remediation. This study involves the isolation and screening of a new extremozyme-producing microbe, Proteus mirabilis JB1, for the production of alkaline-pH-stable laccase. A primary OFAT screening tested a broad range of carbon sources (glucose, lactose, xylose, sucrose, starch, glycerol, cellulose, trisodium citrate, sodium acetate), nitrogen sources (ammonium sulfate, sodium nitrate, urea, beef extract, peptone, casein, gelatin), salts (0.1 mM and 0.01 mM) such as CuSO₄, KCl, ZnCl₂, MgCl₂, MnCl₂, NiCl₂, NaCl, and CaCl₂, and pH levels (7–10). The highest enzyme activity of 0.999 U/ml was achieved using 0.25% (w/v) cellulose, 0.8% (w/v) urea, 0.1 mM MnCl 2 , MgSO 4 , CaCl 2 , NaCl, and KCl, and 0.01 mM CuSO 4 , FeSO 4 , and NiCl 2 at pH 9 with good stability to surfactants (Tween 80, SDS), organic solvents (acetone, ethanol, methanol), and inhibitors (EDTA). PBD and CCD were then implemented to screen and optimize critical parameters—cellulose (1.5% w/v), urea (0.7% w/v), and MgSO₄ (0.05 mM)—to achieve an efficient increase in enzyme activity to 2.3 U/mL, demonstrating the strength and efficacy of the optimization process. Biogenic selenium nanoparticles (Bio-SeNPs) were fabricated and exhibited very high efficiency in pesticide degradation, achieving 100% degradation of cypermethrin without forming any toxic intermediates within 72 h. This research has provided a comprehensive and replicable technique covering microbial isolation, enzyme optimization, fabrication of a nanobiocatalyst, and its application. Key points • A novel isolate, Proteus mirabilis, was employed for the production of the extremozyme laccase. • Optimization increased the yield by 9.58-fold. • Bio-SeNPs were employed to degrade cypermethrin, achieving 100% detoxification within 72 h.

works.title: Colorimetric polymerase spiral reaction (PSR) assay for the rapid detection of hepatitis B virus
works.abstract: Abstract Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection remains a significant global health concern, particularly in low-resource settings with limited access to sophisticated diagnostic tools. Conventional molecular diagnostic assays, such as qPCR, are often restricted to centralized laboratories in urban settings due to their high cost and the need for skilled personnel. This limits its use in lower levels of the healthcare system, highlighting the need for affordable point-of-care (PoC) assays. In this study, we have developed a visual detection method for HBV using a polymerase spiral reaction (PSR) incorporated with hydroxy naphthol blue (HNB) dye. A set of primers was designed targeting a specific region of the S gene of HBV, and the reaction runs in an isothermal condition. The assay conditions were optimized, and the optimal reaction temperature and time were 63 °C and 60 min, respectively. This developed HBV-PSR assay showed a detection limit of 5.04 copies, reaching 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity in clinical evaluation ( n = 85), and colorimetric visualization in 60 min by naked eye. The specificity test revealed no cross-reactivity with other hepatitis-causing viruses and the tested non-HBV pathogens. The assay was tested with 45 HBV-positive clinical samples, which were initially screened by a serological test, and showed a good concordance rate and diagnostic reliability. The HBV-PSR assay designed in this study could potentially be used as a point-of-care diagnostic tool for HBV detection, aiming at early surveillance and detection, focusing on healthcare in poor-resource settings. The combination of isothermal amplification with dye-based visual detection eliminated the need for complex instruments, enabling PoC detection. Key points • A rapid and sensitive PSR assay was developed for HBV detection, with results obtained within 1 h . • HNB dye enabled naked eye visual detection without the need for complex equipment . • The assay detected as few as 5.04 DNA copies and demonstrated high diagnostic performance, outperforming conventional PCR in the evaluated clinical samples .

works.title: Hydrodynamic design space for process transfer across different bioreactor platforms
works.abstract: Abstract The increasing diversification of bioreactor platforms in biopharmaceutical manufacturing, including stirred-tank, 1-D rocking, and orbital-rocking systems, has created challenges for transferring processes across systems with fundamentally different mixing mechanisms. Conventional scale-up parameters, such as power input per unit volume (P/V), are well established for stirred-tank reactors (STRs), but impeller-based methods for estimating P/V are not directly applicable to impeller-free systems. In this study, a computational fluid dynamics (CFD)-based framework was developed to define a hydrodynamic design space for process transfer across stirred-tank (STR), 1-D rocking (RM20), and orbital-rocking (CELBIC50) bioreactor systems. Power dissipation per unit volume (Pd/V) was proposed as a platform-independent energy dissipation parameter and combined with shear stress and mixing time to define feasible operating regions. Using this framework, operating conditions could be identified across different bioreactor types using a multi-constraint hydrodynamic design space. Hydrodynamic analysis revealed distinct flow characteristics among the bioreactors, with CELBIC50 exhibiting lower mean shear stress (0.012 vs. 0.019 Pa) and a shorter mixing time (80.9 vs. 146.6 s) than RM20 under the selected operating conditions. Despite these differences, fed-batch CHO cell cultures under the selected conditions showed comparable cell growth, productivity, metabolite profiles, and product quality across STR 2 L, RM20, and CELBIC50, with most performance variables remaining within the common ± 2 σ range. These results demonstrate that a multi-constraint hydrodynamic design space integrating Pd/V, shear stress, and mixing time provides a quantitative framework for identifying transferable operating conditions across different bioreactor systems and supports model-informed process development. Key points • Hydrodynamic characteristics were systematically compared across stirred-tank, 1-D rocking-motion, and orbital-rocking bioreactors under diverse operating conditions. • Pd/V was proposed as a platform-independent energy dissipation parameter across different bioreactor systems. • A constraint-based hydrodynamic design space integrating Pd/V, shear stress, and mixing time was developed for systematic bioprocess transfer.

works.title: Development of a hybrid machine learning model based on reaction rates for a whole cell biotransformation process
works.abstract: Data-driven or hybrid models can potentially be used to predict the behaviour of complex bioprocesses. In this study, we consider the whole cell biotransformation of oripavine to nororipavine, an N -demethylation step in the production of buprenorphine, where cell growth occurs simultaneously with enzymatic transformation and mechanistic understanding is not yet complete. Data-driven machine learning approaches, including artificial neural networks and recurrent neural networks, were assessed for their ability to predict cell growth, as well as reaction progress from simple online process measurements. Hybrid models were also developed and compared, together with simpler multivariable linear regression. A mass balance was used to pre-process training data for the hybrid model, unknown parameters were then predicted and used to calculate nororipavine concentration. A second rates-based hybrid model predicted the unknown rates of production and consumption of nororipavine, which were then used in a mass balance to predict nororipavine concentration. The hybrid model incorporating a rates-based approach was able to predict process metrics, including the transient peak in nororipavine concentration. The simpler hybrid model, or the data-driven approaches with no mechanistic detail, could not accurately predict nororipavine concentration, only oripavine concentration and cell growth, with the simpler multivariable linear regression only able to predict cell growth. The successful rates-based hybrid model demonstrates a proof-of-concept that could potentially be used for process prediction and monitoring, to supplement offline analytical methods, to provide new data on by-product formation or to simulate process data and improve process control. The study demonstrates the utility of hybrid models, where data-driven components describe complex process behaviour, while mechanistic components with known process knowledge increase model accuracy.

Metabolic impact of redox perturbations on recombinant protein production in Komagataella phaffii under methanolic growth conditions
works.abstract: Recombinant protein extracellular production is a highly demanding process in terms of energy and redox cofactor regeneration. Yeasts such as Komagataella phaffii (aka. Pichia pastoris ) seem to adapt their metabolism by increasing ATP, NADH or NADPH regeneration to compensate for the metabolic burden exerted by such costly process. Earlier studies have proven that increased NADPH regeneration capacity has a positive effect on recombinant protein production when using glucose as sole carbon source, while counteracting increased NADH/NAD + ratios has also been proven beneficial. To evaluate the metabolic impact of increasing NADPH and/or NAD + regeneration caused by the introduction of a cytosolic NADH kinase and an alternative NADH oxidase, we initially performed in silico simulations based on the use of a genome-scale model. Next, we investigated the effect of overexpressing the S. cerevisiae ’s POS5 NADH kinase encoding gene (targeted to the cytosol) and an alternative oxidase ( AtOX ) in a K. phaffii strain producing extracellularly a Rhizopus oryzae lipase (Rol) under control of the alcohol oxidase 1 ( AOX1 ) promoter (P AOX1 ), thereby assessing the impact of such engineering strategies on recombinant protein production and cell performance under methanol growth conditions. Small-scale cultures allowed us to conclude that such genetic modifications increase protein production significantly under methanol growth conditions. The redox-engineered strains were further characterized in bioreactor chemostat cultures using a glucose/methanol mix (60/40%, w/w) as a carbon source to corroborate their performance. Thereby, up to a 36% increase in Rol specific productivity was observed when overexpressing two copies of POS5 , whereas AtOX overexpression did not improve production. Notably, combined two-copy POS5 and AtOX overexpression resulted in a 53% increase in lipase production compared to the reference strain, suggesting that perturbation of the NADH/NAD + ratio leads to widespread changes in metabolism ultimately affecting cell growth and product formation, resulting in the observed additive effect. An in-silico interpretation of the physiological macroscopic data from chemostat cultures using a genome-scale metabolic model allowed us to gain further insights on the metabolic impact of these modifications. Our study provides a DBTL cycle workflow generating valuable insights for a quantitative understanding and prediction of cellular response to redox- based perturbations and subsequent test bedding of metabolic engineering applications in K. phaffii .

works.title: Systematic prioritization of high-value natural ingredients produced by endophytic fungi: technical limitations and market opportunities
works.abstract: Endophytic fungi are a valuable source of natural ingredients with applications in various industries, such as the pharmaceutical, food, cosmetics, and agricultural sectors. Despite the growing number of metabolites reported over the past two decades, the available information on their production is fragmented, which has delayed the entry of these ingredients into various markets. For this reason, this study presents a systematic and critical prioritization of ten high-value ingredients with potential for production by endophytic fungi. The catalog was created based on a structured literature review, combined with a process of screening information to compile the reported secondary metabolites and crude extracts. Subsequently, each ingredient was evaluated based on criteria such as substrate availability and cost, market demand and competitiveness, potential as a building block, the technological maturity of the production process, and regulatory complexity. As a result, the ten most promising ingredients were selected: Brefeldin A, chrysin, emodin, huperzine A, paclitaxel, podophyllotoxin, quercetin, resveratrol, vinblastine, and vincristine are the compounds with the greatest potential for production from endophytic fungi. This article includes information on their bioactivities, the fungi that produce them, the state of fermentation, the operating mode, reactor configurations, and culture media. An analysis of the progress made in each of the production processes reveals that challenges remain in terms of optimization, scaling up, and regulatory approval for certain ingredients. Thus, this study provides a systematic prioritization framework that can guide future research, support decision-making in bioprocess design, and accelerate the establishment of a competitive industry based on fungal ingredients.

works.title: Biomass conversion in thermo‐catalytic reforming reactor: process modeling and kinetic insights for integrated intermediate pyrolysis
works.abstract: Abstract A sustainable energy transition in the 21st century necessitates efficient biomass‐to‐energy conversion technologies, with pyrolysis playing a crucial role. Thermo‐catalytic reforming (TCR) combines intermediate pyrolysis with a catalytic post‐reforming stage, producing higher‐quality bio‐oil, char, and syngas than conventional pyrolysis. However, process models capable of predicting TCR performance across different feedstocks remain limited. This work presents an Aspen Plus‐based kinetic process model that couples both TCR reaction stages, primary pyrolysis, and catalytic post‐reforming, within a single framework. The model integrates the CRECK kinetic mechanism with a detailed char decomposition model, predicting product yields and gas composition directly from feedstock elemental analysis. It is validated against experimental data from five compositionally distinct feedstocks: digestate, municipal solid waste, eucalyptus, bagasse, and straw pellets. These span both conventional lignocellulosic biomass and heterogeneous waste streams. The model achieves strong agreement for char yield predictions across all five feedstocks, within approximately 1–2% deviation, while bio‐oil prediction accuracy varies by feedstock composition. Sensitivity analysis of post‐reformer temperature (800–900 °C) shows a consistent increase in H 2 (by approximately 8–12%) and decrease in CH 4 (by approximately 23–46%) across all feedstocks. This trend is driven by steam methane reforming and water–gas shift conversion, identifying higher post‐reformer temperature as a generalizable route to improved syngas quality. The model requires only standard elemental feedstock analysis as input, linking feedstock composition directly to predicted product distribution and enabling identification of favorable operating conditions ahead of physical trials.

Modular microfluidic device for intensified CAR T cell expansion
works.abstract: Autologous Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) T cell manufacturing remains costly and labour-intensive, with workflows reliant on manual interventions despite advances in automation. Here, we present a compact microfluidic cell culture device (µCCD) with a simple, modular architecture for intensified CAR T cell expansion. Over four days, the µCCD yielded 10.5 × 10⁶ viable primary T cells compared with 49.8 × 10⁶ viable cells in the G-Rex®, while achieving a 6.7-fold higher viable cell concentration. For CAR T cells, the µCCD achieved a 14-fold expansion, yielding 14.1 × 10⁶ viable cells, compared with 25.1 × 10⁶ viable cells in the G-Rex®, and reaching 56.5×10 6 viable cells·mL -1 – a concentration seldom achieved in conventional culture systems and 18-fold higher than a G-Rex® well-based static culture control. Continuous perfusion maintained glucose availability, while integrated oxygen sensors enabled real-time monitoring. Expanded CAR T cells retained cytotoxic activity comparable to G-Rex®-expanded cells under the tested conditions, and microfluidic culture yielded a higher proportion of central memory CAR T cells, which are associated with long-term therapeutic persistence. The platform's modular architecture and low seeding requirement provide a foundation for future clinical-dose manufacturing and rapid assessment of patient-to-patient variability. Together, these results demonstrate the feasibility of the µCCD as a compact and adaptable platform for the high-density expansion of functionally robust CAR T cells. By demonstrating that a modular microfluidic architecture can support the expansion of non-adherent therapeutic cell cultures, this work represents an important step towards more standardised microfluidic platforms for next-generation cell therapy manufacturing.

works.title: Green solvent‐based reactive extraction of glutaric acid: performance of natural oils in tri‐n‐butyl phosphate
works.abstract: Abstract Background Recovery of glutaric acid from dilute aqueous streams such as fermentation broths and process wastewaters remains challenging because of its high water solubility and the high cost of conventional downstream separation. This study investigates the reactive extraction of glutaric acid using tri‐ n ‐butyl phosphate (TBP) dissolved in green vegetable oils, namely sunflower, soybean, and sesame oils. Results The extraction performance was evaluated in terms of the distribution coefficient ( K D ), extraction efficiency ( E %), equilibrium complexation constant ( K E ), and loading ratio ( z ). At the highest TBP concentration (3.614 mol L −1 ), sunflower oil exhibited the highest extraction performance, with a maximum distribution coefficient of 4.61 and extraction efficiency of 85.9%, followed by soybean oil ( K D = 4.61, E = 82.2%) and sesame oil ( K D = 3.59, E = 78.15%). The diffusivity of glutaric acid towards the organic‐aqueous interface was estimated as 1.78 × 10 −6 cm 2 s −1 using the Wilke‐Chang equation and 2.02 × 10 −6 cm 2 s −1 using the Reddy‐Doraiswamy correlation. The minimum solvent‐to‐feed ( S / F ) ratio and the required number of theoretical stages for counter‐current extraction were determined from the equilibrium data, while negligible water co‐extraction confirmed the hydrophobic nature of the vegetable oils. Conclusion Reactive extraction of glutaric acid using TBP in vegetable oils demonstrated that sunflower oil was the most effective green diluent, followed by soybean oil and sesame oil. The diffusivity data and process design parameters obtained in this study provide useful information for the design and scale‐up of continuous reactive extraction systems for sustainable glutaric acid recovery. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry (SCI).

works.title: Effect of enzyme-support interactions on the catalytic behavior of lipases immobilized on magnetic graphene oxide
works.abstract: Understanding enzyme-support interactions is essential for the rational design of immobilized biocatalysts with enhanced activity and stability. This study investigated lipase immobilization by physical adsorption onto graphene oxide modified with superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles (SPION+GO). Five commercial lipases were screened, and Thermomyces lanuginosus lipase (TLL) exhibited the highest specific activity, being selected for further investigation. The immobilized biocatalyst (SPION+GO+TLL) showed 37% higher esterification activity than the free enzyme, together with improved thermal stability and extended half-life. Adsorption promoted favorable enzyme-support interactions that stabilized the active conformation while preserving the flexibility required for catalysis. However, only limited improvements in pH tolerance were observed, indicating that the non-covalent interactions established on the non-functionalized graphene oxide surface were insufficient to ensure enzyme stabilization under different protonation conditions. Opposite catalytic behaviors were also observed under different ethanol hydration conditions: free TLL performed better with hydrated ethanol, whereas the immobilized enzyme was more active in anhydrous ethanol, suggesting that the SPION+GO support created a protective microenvironment for reactions under low-water conditions. These findings demonstrate that enzyme-support interactions, rather than the support itself, govern immobilized lipase performance and provide guidance for developing graphene-based magnetic biocatalysts for biodiesel synthesis and other non-aqueous biocatalytic processes.

Development of activated biocarbons from wild fruit processing residues via direct activation with CO₂: Evaluation of temperature and heating mode effects
works.abstract: This study investigates the development and characterization of activated biocarbons produced from elderberry, hawthorn, and rowan processing residues via direct activation with CO₂. The effect of activation temperature (700 and 800 °C) and heating mode (conventional and microwave-assisted) on the physicochemical and adsorption properties of the obtained materials was systematically evaluated. The activated biocarbons were characterized in terms of textural parameters, morphology, elemental composition, as well as surface acid–base and electrokinetic properties. Their adsorption capacity towards three nonionic organic pollutants - poly(vinylpyrrolidone), Triton X-100, and Disperse Yellow 211 - was assessed. The obtained materials were characterized by a predominantly basic surface character and a moderately developed specific surface area ranging from 82 to 485 m² g⁻¹, with micropores constituting the dominant fraction of the porous structure. This type of pore structure did not favor the adsorption of macromolecular compounds, resulting in a relatively low adsorption capacity. The adsorption capacity under the applied experimental conditions reached 5.80 mg g⁻¹ for poly(vinylpyrrolidone), 16.08 mg g⁻¹ for Triton X-100, and 12.04 mg g⁻¹ for Disperse Yellow 211, with the highest values obtained for the biocarbons activated at 800 °C using microwave-assisted heating. The stability of aqueous suspensions of the obtained materials and the influence of the nonionic polymer on these systems were also investigated. Depending on the type of activated biocarbon, either stabilization or destabilization of the suspension was observed.

works.title: Integrating dynamic modeling and continuous cultivation to enhance recombinant β-glucosidase production in Komagataella phaffii
works.abstract: Cultivation under hypothermia has emerged as an interesting strategy for enhancing recombinant protein production in Komagataella phaffii , yet predictive approaches capable of integrating the effects of temperature and cell growth rate for rational bioprocess optimization remain limited. In this work, we investigated the influence of cultivation temperature on recombinant β-glucosidase (BGL1) production in the hybrid K. phaffii strain S467 by combining bioprocess characterization with dynamic mathematical modeling. Batch cultures performed at 20, 25 and 30 °C showed that hypothermia increased recombinant protein secretion while reducing biomass formation, revealing a trade-off between cell growth and product formation. To quantitatively describe these dynamics, a Droop-based model incorporating delayed coupling between substrate uptake and biomass synthesis was fitted using the experimental data. Model simulations predicted that continuous cultivation at 20 °C and a dilution rate of 0.045 h −1 maximized the total secreted protein volumetric productivity. Chemostat experiments at selected conditions yielded biomass concentrations and total secreted protein productivities close to the simulated values, supporting the model-predicted trends and its potential as a tool for process optimization. Interestingly, the highest specific BGL1 activity was observed at the highest dilution rate despite a lower bgl1 transcript level and secreted protein production, suggesting that cultivation conditions influence recombinant protein traits through mechanisms beyond transcriptional regulation. Collectively, these results show that integrating experimental bioprocess characterization, predictive dynamic modeling and targeted molecular analyses provide an effective framework for rational optimization of recombinant protein production in this biotechnologically relevant yeast.

works.title: De novo biosynthesis of the plant-derived aloe-emodin in Aspergillus nidulans via artificial pathway assembly and temporal flux control
Late-stage large extracellular vesicles reprogram CHO cell metabolism in a glutamine-dependent mode and promote antibody-productivity to cell-growth tradeoff
works.abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are mediators of intercellular communication, yet their impact on Chinese Hamster Ovary (CHO) cell physiology and bioprocess performance remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated whether small EVs (sEVs) and large EVs (LgEVs) that accumulate during fed-batch and perfusion cultures modulate CHO cell growth, metabolism, apoptosis, and monoclonal antibody (mAb) production. EVs isolated from early- and late-stage cultures were added to fresh CHO cultures grown with or without glutamine supplementation. Only LgEVs had a significant impact. Late-stage LgEVs markedly altered CHO-cell behavior, reducing cell proliferation, increasing apoptosis under glutamine-limited conditions, and substantially enhancing mAb productivity in a dose-dependent manner. Glutamine supplementation largely alleviated the growth-inhibitory and pro-apoptotic effects of LgEVs while preserving their positive impact on productivity, suggesting that glutamine mitigated the EV-mediated stress without affecting the productivity enhancement. Metabolic analyses revealed increased glucose consumption, an enhanced glutamine-dependent shift between glycine and alanine overflow metabolism, and remodeling of amino-acid utilization. Metabolic flux analysis further demonstrated enhanced glycolytic overflow and increased reliance on amino acid-supported anaplerosis. Conversely, selective removal of LgEVs from perfusion medium significantly improved cell expansion without reducing antibody production, supporting an inhibitory role for late-stage LgEVs. These LgEVs were enriched in let-7 family miRNAs and miR-21, consistent with RNAseq analyses demonstrating stress-associated enrichment of these miRNAs in CHO EVs and with functional studies showing that let-7a and miR-21 reduce CHO-cell growth. Together, these observations suggest that selective miRNA loading contributes to the growth, metabolic, and productivity phenotypes elicited by late-stage LgEVs. Our findings identify LgEVs in CHO-K1 can act as endogenous regulators of CHO-cell physiology thus deserving attention for optimizing high-density fed-batch and perfusion biomanufacturing processes.

works.title: Comparison of synthetic and post-synthetic molecular genetic methods of reducing xylan glucuronidation in hybrid aspen for biorefinery applications
works.abstract: BACKGROUND: The pattern of xylan backbone substitution by 4-O-methylglucuronic acid (mGlcA) and O-acetyl groups generated during biosynthesis in the Golgi apparatus plays a key role in molecular interactions between secondary cell wall polymers in hardwoods, thus regulating biorefinery properties of woody biomass. This study aims at comparing the effects of two different approaches to reduce xylan glucuronidation, targeting either xylan biosynthesis by RNAi suppression of GLUCURONIC SUBSTITUTION OF XYLAN1 genes (denoted Gux1RNAi) or by xylan post-synthetic modification in the secondary cell wall by apoplastic wood-specific expression of a fungal α-glucuronidase from family GH67 (denoted WP:GH67) in hybrid aspen (Populus tremula L. x tremuloides Michx.). The effects of reducing xylan glucuronidation by these two approaches on xylan acetylation and solubility, and recalcitrance of wood to enzymatic hydrolysis were compared. RESULTS: Both approaches reduced mGlcA/xylose (Xyl) ratio by approx. 30% without altering Xyl content in alkali extracts, while xylan acetyl content in subcritical water extracts was increased only in Gux1RNAi lines. The Gux1RNAi lines showed reduced glucuronidation in the major xylan domain containing evenly-spaced mGlcA, whereas the WP:GH67 lines were affected in both odd and even glucuronidation patterns. Interestingly, the arrays containing mGlcA every second xylosyl unit were not affected by any modification, whereas an increase in xylo-oligosaccharides containing O-2,3 diacetylated Xyl was found in Gux1RNAi lines only. Neither modification consistently affected glucose or Xyl yields in saccharification without or with acid pretreatment, whereas xylan extractability in subcritical water was increased in Gux1RNAi, but not in WP:GH67 lines. CONCLUSION: Our study supports the hypothesis that acetylation competes with glucuronidation by GUX1 during biosynthesis, and increased acetylation caused by GUX1 suppression rather than reduced xylan glucuronidation per se improves xylan extractability. The 30% reduction in glucuronidation did not affect enzymatic saccharification, supporting the concept that cell wall structure and recalcitrance in transgenic lines are maintained by xylan domains which were not affected by either transgenic modification.

works.title: Metabolic engineering of Methylorubrum extorquens PA1 for cinnamic acid production from ethanol
works.abstract: Developing a microbial platform capable of converting ethanol into value-added products is vital for next-generation carbon recycling biorefineries. Methylorubrum extorquens PA1 is a facultative methylotroph that assimilates ethanol; however, its metabolic potential for aromatic synthesis from ethanol has not been explored. Here, we report the first demonstration of de novo cinnamic acid (CA) production from ethanol in a methylotrophic bacterium. Metabolite profiling revealed that ethanol assimilation was limited by inefficient conversion of acetate to acetyl-CoA. Overexpression of endogenous acetyl-CoA synthase (MeACS1) suppressed extracellular acetate accumulation and improved growth on ethanol. To establish the CA biosynthetic module, we introduced Streptomyces maritimus phenylalanine ammonia-lyase (SmEncP), enabling conversion of L-phenylalanine into CA. To enhance precursor supply, we strengthened the shikimate pathway and phenylalanine biosynthetic pathway by co-expressing feedback-resistant 3-deoxy-D-arabino-heptulosonate-7-phosphate synthase (EcAroG fbr ) and chorismate mutase/prephenate dehydrogenase (EcPheA fbr ) from Escherichia coli . Further, endogenous transketolase (MeTkt) was overexpressed to enhance erythrose-4-phosphate supply. The resulting strain PAc1/pTE102-CA3 produced 1.75 mg L⁻ 1 of CA from ethanol in test tube culture, 2.6-fold that obtained from methanol. Fed-batch cultivation with ethanol feeding achieved 52.34 mg L⁻ 1 of CA, demonstrating stable conversion of ethanol to value-added chemicals without notable growth inhibition or acetate accumulation. This study establishes M. extorquens PA1 as a promising chassis for ethanol-based aromatic biosynthesis and suggests that relieving acetyl-CoA bottlenecks is likely critical for efficient ethanol assimilation. This work provides ethanol-driven aromatic biosynthesis in methylotrophs and offers a foundation for further engineering of C₂-assimilating bacteria toward renewable chemical production.

works.title: Genomic and phenotypic characterization of Vibrio proteolyticus and its postbiotic potential
works.abstract: Abstract Vibrio proteolyticus DCF12.2, isolated from the intestinal tract of the flatfish Dicologlossa cuneata , was characterized through integrated genomic and phenotypic analyses to assess its antimicrobial activity, biosynthetic potential and resistance- and virulence-related features. Genome-based analyses supported its assignment to V. proteolyticus and identified biosynthetic gene clusters associated with arylpolyene, nonribosomal peptide (NRP)-metallophore/amphibactin, ectoine and ribosomally synthesized and posttranslationally modified peptide/nonribosomal peptide synthetase (RiPP-/NRPS)-like pathways, together with numerous predicted antimicrobial peptide candidates. The resistome was mainly composed of chromosomal efflux- and target-associated determinants, whereas virulence-related hits were largely restricted to functions linked to motility, chemotaxis and secretion. The genome also contained sequences homologous to proteins previously described in Photobacterium damselae subsp. piscicida and Vibrio harveyi , as well as three prophage regions and multiple genomic islands (GIs). Phenotypic assays showed that the strain and/or its extracellular products (ECPs) inhibited P. damselae subsp. damselae , V. harveyi and Aeromonas hydrophila . The inhibitory activity of the ECPs against P. damselae subsp. damselae was maintained after incubation at 37 °C and after acidification to pH 5. In conclusion, although the strain exhibits antimicrobial activity and other characteristics that would qualify it a probiotic candidate, the presence of certain virulence factors makes it more suitable for use as a postbiotic. Key points DCF12.2 shows broad genomic potential for antimicrobial compound production Extracellular products inhibit relevant aquatic bacterial pathogens Virulence-related traits support postbiotic rather than probiotic use

works.title: Interkingdom communication 2.0: pheromone-based control between Bacillus subtilis and Saccharomyces cerevisiae
works.abstract: Microbial communities found in nature are complex and thrive in harmony, consisting of organisms derived from several kingdoms. Hence, they need to be able to communicate by quorum-sensing molecules to co-exist in close proximity. Being able to engineer artificial interkingdom communication for biotechnological approaches, such as degradation of complex biomaterials in one fermenter using controlled signaling between microorganisms, would be beneficial. Therefore, we wanted to establish a proof of principle by enabling the Gram-positive bacterium Bacillus subtilis to communicate in a controlled manner with the eukaryotic yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae by exploiting the yeast's pheromone system. We genetically modified B. subtilis to heterologously produce the α-pheromone after bacitracin induction, which in turn would activate the production of the green fluorescent protein mNeongreen upon pheromone recognition by S. cerevisiae. Co-cultivation in modified growth medium and induction of pheromone expression was successful and repeatable. Yeast activation and production of mNeongreen was visible not only by analysis but also by epifluorescence microscopy of the co-culture. This study successfully demonstrated controlled interkingdom signaling between microorganisms by leveraging their native communication systems. KEY POINTS: • Heterologous production and secretion of small peptides in Bacillus subtilis. • Interkingdom communication between bacteria and yeast. • Signaling by artificially produced pheromones.

works.title: Butyrate production from the simultaneous utilization of carbon monoxide and acetate in Eubacterium-dominated enrichments
works.abstract: Abstract Syngas conversion to carboxylic acids can be achieved through the combined actions of acetogens and chain elongators. Mixed cultures enriched with these functional groups can serve as robust and resilient catalysts for bio-based production, but developing efficient and stable communities remains challenging. In this study, we aimed to enrich a mixed microbial culture for efficient syngas-driven chain elongation using carbon monoxide (CO) and acetate as substrates. Three strategies were employed: (i) conventional enrichment using anaerobic sludge only, (ii) sludge augmentation with known syngas fermenters (Clostridium autoethanogenum, Clostridium carboxidivorans, Eubacterium limosum, and Acetobacterium wieringae) to enhance carboxydotrophic activity, and (iii) sludge augmentation with chain elongator Clostridium kluyveri to stimulate chain elongation. Enrichments were performed in batch cultures with stepwise increases in CO partial pressure across successive transfers until a 100% CO (170 kPa) headspace was reached. Ultimately, all enrichments grew under a 100% CO headspace, simultaneously utilizing CO and acetate, with butyrate as main product. 16S rRNA gene and metagenomic analyses revealed that Eubacterium became predominant. Several genera (Aminobacterium, Anaerotignum, Oscillibacter, and Proteiniphilum) not known to ferment CO, were also enriched. Based on physiological and metagenomic analyses, we hypothesize that Eubacterium consumes CO and acetate, producing butyrate and extracellular polymeric substance (EPS)-like material. Metagenomic data further suggests that components derived from this EPS-like material may serve as substrate for the other enriched genera. This study demonstrates that augmentation can steer mixed microbial communities toward targeted product formation and highlights the critical role of initial culture conditions in shaping community composition and functionality. Key points • Mixed cultures converted CO and acetate mainly to butyrate under a 100% CO headspace. • Acetogen augmentation to a mixed community shortened lag-phase in the presence of CO. • Metagenomics suggests microbial use of sugars and amino acids from EPS-like material.

works.title: Sustainable polymer‐based composites for fused granular fabrication in large‐format additive manufacturing reinforced with lignocellulose derived from agroforestry and industrial waste: a critical review and technical outlook
works.abstract: Abstract Lignocellulosic‐reinforced polymers (LRPs) derived from agroforestry and industrial residues offer a promising route to reduce fossil‐polymer consumption and valorize residual biomass in fused granular fabrication (FGF) for large‐format additive manufacturing (LFAM). However, available knowledge remains fragmented across feedstock selection, composite formulation, interfacial modification, processing, performance evaluation, and industrial implementation. This review therefore critically examines the complete development chain of LRPs for FGF‐based LFAM, including lignocellulosic feedstocks and polymer matrices, pretreatment and surface‐modification strategies, compatibilization, compounding and fabrication conditions, and the resulting physical, mechanical, thermal, rheological, interfacial, and durability‐related properties. Particular attention is also given to application sectors, recyclability, environmental assessment, and technology readiness. The reviewed evidence shows that lignocellulosic reinforcements can reduce composite density, increase stiffness, and support the substitution of virgin polymer, but their moisture sensitivity, thermal instability, variable morphology, and limited matrix compatibility can impair extrusion stability, inter‐bead consolidation, dimensional accuracy, and long‐term performance. Surface modification and compatibilization improve interfacial adhesion, although their benefits depend strongly on the reinforcement–matrix–processing combination. Demonstrated applications include lighting products, furniture and interior‐design items, packaging, and decorative household products. The technology‐readiness assessment indicates that most academic studies are positioned at an estimated technology‐readiness level (TRLe) of 3–5, whereas the most advanced industrial initiatives assessed reach approximately TRLe 6–7, with scalability, durability validation, regulatory qualification, market integration, and life‐cycle assessment remaining the principal bottlenecks. Future progress requires standardized feedstock characterization, process monitoring, application‐specific qualification, circularity assessment, and coordinated academia–industry scale‐up.

works.title: Kikuyu grass clippings as a bioeconomy feedstock: influence of pyrolysis conditions on biochar properties and its effect on the growth of Swiss chard
works.abstract: Abstract The integration of urban organic waste streams into the bioeconomy is critical for advancing the water–food–energy nexus. Grass clippings, an abundant and underutilized municipal residue, represent a promising feedstock for producing value‐added materials. This study provides a comprehensive evaluation of biochar produced from Kikuyu grass ( Cenchrus clandestinus ) and its potential for soil amendment and carbon sequestration. Biochar was produced by slow pyrolysis under nitrogen, examining the effects of two feedstock particle sizes and three peak temperatures (400, 500, and 600 °C). Higher pyrolysis temperatures increased biochar pH and the abundance of aromatic carbon structures, but decreased biochar yields correspondingly. The maximum specific surface area was achieved at 500 °C using the larger feedstock size fraction. Expanding upon preliminary findings, this study established a direct, positive correlation between biochar surface area and both water retention capacity and CO 2 adsorption capacity, demonstrating the dual benefits of climate mitigation and soil improvement. The performance of selected biochars as soil conditioners was assessed in a greenhouse trial with Swiss chard ( Beta vulgaris ). Biochar application improved soil water retention and enhanced plant growth significantly compared with untreated controls. Preliminary cost considerations, based on published fertilizer prices, suggest that biochar may offer long‐term economic advantages through soil benefits extending over multiple growing seasons. However, field‐scale validation is required to confirm profitability because the present greenhouse study was not designed as a formal techno‐economic analysis. These findings highlight the potential for valorizing urban grass clippings into biochar as a viable pathway within the circular bioeconomy, contributing to waste reduction, soil improvement, and long‐term carbon sequestration.

works.title: Advances in lemon peel‐based adsorbents for wastewater treatment applications
works.abstract: Abstract Water pollution threatens the environment and human health. Treatment methods must be sustainable and affordable. Lemon peel‐based adsorbents offer a practical option for wastewater treatment. This review assesses their preparation, performance, mechanisms, and application. The adsorbents were classified into lemon peel biosorbents, activated carbon, biochar, and composites. Adsorbent modification was found to improve performance. Chemically modified lemon peel adsorbents achieved high maximum adsorption capacities, particularly for lead(II), among the heavy metals reviewed, with performance influenced by pH, adsorbent dosage, temperature, initial pollutant concentration, and contact time. Most systems followed Langmuir isotherms and pseudo‐second‐order kinetics. These patterns point to chemisorption dominated by ion exchange, electrostatic attraction, and hydrogen bonding. Thermodynamic analysis showed negative Gibbs free energy values, indicating spontaneous processes. Regeneration tests showed that appreciable adsorption capacity was retained after repeated cycles. Competitive adsorption showed strong selectivity with little interference from common ions. Mechanistic studies showed multiple adsorption pathways, including surface complexation, which binds metals to oxygen‐containing groups; π–π stacking, which secures aromatic pollutants; and electrostatic forces, which attract charged species. Lemon peel‐based adsorbents provide low‐cost and environmentally friendly alternatives for wastewater treatment. They convert agricultural waste into useful treatment materials. Such conversion supports waste valorization and circular economy principles while addressing global water quality challenges.

works.title: Rare earth element biosensing in chemically complex waters: Interference mechanisms, operating windows, and mitigation for a lanmodulin enzymatic switch
works.abstract: Rare earth elements (REE) are increasingly mobilised from mine residues and other industrial sources, creating a need for rapid screening of chemically complex waters where conventional ICP-based analysis is impractical on site. Here, we evaluate a lanthanide-gated enzymatic switch biosensor, for matrix-aware monitoring of mine-influenced waters. We quantified REE-dependent activation and systematic interference from co-occurring metals and anions typical of mine waters, and defined operating windows that preserve lanthanide responsiveness. REE activation was readily detectable at ~100 nM, whereas inhibition emerged in the low-micromolar range and became pronounced near ~10 µM for key interferents, corresponding to a practical tolerance of roughly 1:100 (REE:inhibiting element). Inhibition was strongest for Al III , Fe III , Ga III , Zn II , and Sn II . Combined machine learning, molecular dynamics, and density functional theory analyses indicate distinct inhibition modes, including coordination of Fe III , Zn II , and Sn II at the LanM EF4 hand loop and favourable binding of [Al(OH) 4 ] - /[Ga(OH) 4 ] - near the TEM-1 substrate-recognition region. Consistent with these predictions, citrate reduced inhibition from hydrolysing metals, especially Al III and Sn II . Together, these findings define matrix-dependent operating envelopes, mechanistic design rules, and practical mitigation strategies for deploying REE biosensors in chemically complex waters.

feeds.summary:
Abstract

Fucoidan and fucosylated xyloglucan are naturally abundant polysaccharides that can serve as α-l-fucosyl donors. feeds.summary:
Abstract
                     African swine fever (ASF), caused by ASF virus (ASFV), poses a significant threat to global swine industries due to its high mortality and the lack of an effective vaccine. Consequently, it is critical to develop a rapid and quantitative detection method for timely monitoring of swine populations and accurate confirmation of ASF infection, thereby enhancing ASF prevention and control measures. feeds.summary:
Abstract

feeds.summary:
Abstract
                Acetate has a considerable potential as a non-food feedstock for microbial bioproduction, yet its use for amino acid production remains underexplored. Here, we developed a process for L-threonine production from acetate as the sole carbon source with Corynebacterium glutamicum by integrating rational, genome-based metabolic engineering with pH-coupled fed-batch cultivation. The engineered strain AT-3 carried five chromosomal mutations that alleviated feedback inhibition of key enzymes and redirected carbon flux toward the aspartate pathway. Abstract

feeds.summary:
Abstract
                     Fungi are prolific producers of chemically diverse natural products and biocatalytically active enzymes, yet the biosynthetic and biotransformation potential of many fungal species remains underexplored. This study establishes Rhizopus stolonifer as a promising platform for both natural-product discovery and selective biotransformation of bioactive molecules. feeds.summary:
Abstract

feeds.summary:
Abstract
                     Gluten, the main storage protein in wheat, barley, and rye, contains sequences rich in proline and glutamine that resist complete gastrointestinal degradation resulting in generation of immunogenic peptides. Abstract
                Despite its industrial importance, microbial L-lysine production has largely been confined to classical producer strains, leaving the fast-growing, non-pathogenic marine bacterium V. natriegens mostly unexplored as an emerging biosynthetic platform. feeds.summary:
Abstract
                     Zearalenone (ZEA) is a Fusarium-derived mycotoxin that contaminates cereal crops and persists in soils and aquatic environments. feeds.summary:
Abstract

feeds.summary: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is a leading cause of global cancer mortality. feeds.summary:
Abstract
                     Nanoscience has revolutionized materials synthesis, with noble metal nanoparticles like silver and gold gaining prominence for their unique physicochemical and biological properties. feeds.summary:
Abstract
                     Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD), predominantly caused by serotype O foot-and-mouth disease virus (FMDV), remains highly contagious and economically devastating worldwide. A significant challenge in disease control is that recovered or vaccinated animals can become asymptomatic carriers of persistent strains (Op), which are indistinguishable from acute wild-type (WT) strains using current diagnostic methods. feeds.summary:
Abstract
                     A handheld, visible near-infrared (VNIR) hyperspectral imaging (HSI) camera was used to differentiate between Listeria species (L. monocytogenes, L. ivanovii and L. innocua) and two L. monocytogenes serotypes: 1/2a and 4b. feeds.title: Sodium Sulfite as an Oxygen-Depletion-Based Chemical Model of Tumor Hypoxia In Vitro
feeds.summary: Hypoxia is a major determinant of tumor progression, yet most chemical hypoxia models rely on HIF stabilization rather than true oxygen depletion. Here, we evaluated sodium sulfite (SS), a direct oxygen scavenger, as an oxygen-dependent in vitro hypoxia model. Cancer cell lines were treated with optimized SS concentrations, and dissolved oxygen levels were monitored for up to 96 h.
